I posted to HN, and then my website was flooded with AI BOT traffic
For the past few years, I've been working on sprinklz.io, a customizable feed reader that can, among other things, deprioritize certain topics from your news feed.
A month ago, I posted it to HN, and it got a hundred or so upvotes, nice! It seems like people are really tired of hearing about LLMs, and they enjoyed being able to deprioritize them from their feed. It was a good demo of why a tool like this is useful. Everything was looking up, and then…
My website got slow. Like, really, painfully slow. At first I chalked it up to the extra attention of a suddenly popular post. Like any developer I both celebrated, and vowed to make my website more resiliant in the future. Strangely though, the slowness continued, and even started to get worse several days after my post went live, and the metrics I did log did not make sense. Like, you know, a good handful of genuinely active, logged-in users, and a sever exhibiting exhorbatantly high load.
So I took a look at some data. I added top-level logging for every endpoint (how many times was a request made to each url path), and I found that a majority of the requests did not even make an attempt to fetch news articles! For reference, my website is built as a single-page-application, and what this means is that a majority of the requests did not even run the javascript necessary to render the page (!).
Digging further, I looked at aggregate NGINX logs to find abusers, and, you're never going to believe this, but it turns out that nearly half of our traffic was coming from one specific user. I won't name names, but I looked them up, and they describe themselves as a service that listens for changes to a website, and then summarizes them into an AI slop news letter. And by 'listens to changes' I mean query our website many many times per-minute. Blocked.
Several of the others were your standard known crawlers, and kindly identified themselves as such. Claude bot, OpenAI bot, google's search indexer, and several others. I even picked up a few vulnerability scanners along the way. At least, somebody is trying to access -/wp-content/phpinfo.php (my website is not a wordpress site). I added robots.txt to discourage most of the AI scanners, but allow google-bot and other search-related traffic, and asked claude to query all the vulnerability paths and mimic the scanners to make sure I wasn't leaking anything. I also added reasonable rate limits, etc., etc.
The most important lesson though, is that it's time to make my website faster. I want to be the website that can day handle xxx QPS of real traffic, and it should scale better than it did, even under heavy load. Inspired by this encounter, I've made quite a few improvements to the underlying infrastructure over the past few weeks, and these should result in pretty substantial performance gains for all users.
P.S. if you'd like to check it out, the website is fully free, and available here
The TLDR is that it lets you define your own customizations, in addition to things like the points totals from hacker news. You can use it to filter out topics, like AI or LLMs, but the topics are completely arbitrary and you can program your own customizations.
Using LLMs to Make the Emacs Web Browser Great Again
When I tell people about the emacs web browser, their first reaction is 'Wait emacs has a web browser?!', followed by, 'yeah… I guess that's kind of a web browser'.
The emacs web browser is designed to render webpages in a terminal-based, textonly environment and, well, it goes about exactly the way you'd expect. It works well on HTML-only, small-content websites, but not so good for anything else.
The problem is that emacs is primarily a text-only editor, but the modern internet is very much not plain-text based. Simple HTML, designed in the simple style of the 1990s has a clear translation into plain text, but modern UI design, with it's visual styling, heavy javascript, and just, overall chaos, not so much.
The emacs web browser would be great, if only we could find a way to go back in time…
Ok, so the plan is simple. We take modern webpages, rewrite their source code into old-school simply-styled HTML, and then pipe it through to the emacs web browser. We just need to find a way to do this easily and at scale.
So um, you didn't forget about LLMs did you? It's nice to be using them in a way that will hopefully reduce the amount of spam content in the world.
Basically, the plan is we write a program that:
Opens a webpage in firefox
Loads the page and runs all the javascript
Asks an LLM to generate a re-usable program that transforms the current-page's contents into simplified text
Inject the generated javascript into the firefox browser
Grab the new page source and forward it to emacs web browser.
Yeah, and so, I've been using it, and it runs very well. Like realistically I can use this on many webpages where eww (emacs web wowser) did not run previously.
Below are some examples of before and after:
The docs for Clojure's mapcat
Figure 1: (before) Using eww-readable
Figure 2: (after) Using simpleweb-simplify-page
It takes a moment to generate the initial modifier program, but once it's generated, it runs pretty fast, and during day-to-day browsing, it mostly doesn't need any extra LLM calls. I have been using it myself and enjoying the experience.
The source code lives here: https://github.com/sstraust/simpleweb
and is open-source, and free to install, etc., etc.
If technology got better, why did everything get worse?
I think we all know the answer to this: bad incentives.
Technology makes systems more productive, but it does not, in fact, make you in particular more productive. The tools that enable computers to be more efficient also enable people to be more efficient at exploiting your time, attention, and wellbeing. I'm talking neural nets babyyy.
I first noticed the problem in 2018. Or rather, I noticed that I had a problem, and that problem was spendinng 3 hours a day watching starcraft 2 replays and wondering where the time went, and how I managed to stay up til 2am again.
What's interesting to me is that I didn't have any of these problems until the late 2010s. I had a computer with an internet connection since at least the mid 2000s, and a smartphone with twitter and reddit and the like not long after. It's possible that I've gotten less resiliant over the years, but I have a sneaking suspiscion that it's the computers who changed.
I can't quite put my finger on it, but I have this sensation that every time I interact with a system or website, I'm playing this kind of adversarial game, where I'm trying to just go about my day, and maybe read a little article about computers, and they're trying to figure out a way to keep me on their site for just a little bit longer.
I also have this feeling that as software engineering has moved from a discipline of hobbyists and enthusiasts to leaders who increasingly developed through finance or business-minded tracks, we've found ourselves with these major tools that we used to love become both extremely bland and extremely profitable.
So what can we do it make it stop?
touch grass. really when the world is like this, i think the best solution is to just leave. it's not easy, especially when the planning is often online, but if you can set it up, I promise that a day in the park playing chess with your friends is better than any amount of time you can spend on the internet.
take to the streets. i think that protesting is effective, and more people should do it. if you're willing to take action, it models to others that they can take action.
stop coming back to the same machines. I think we all have this gamblers fallacy in us, where if it didn't pay out the first time, but it pays out sometimes, we try the machine again, but it doesn't really work like that. if you're losing money the lesson is to stop putting coins in the machine.
editor's note: I've been working on a free customizable news reader as a way to take out some of my frustrations with the modern internet. if you don't use this one, I recommend following individual blogs and websites, because it's so much better to just get off these big platforms entirely.
editors note 2: i haven't yet posted this latest article to my rss xml, because i'm not ready to send notifications for it yet. will add in the coming weeks.
Deft version 0.2.0
Now that deft 0.2.0 is released, I figure it's a good time to talk about what I built, and why I built it.
The point of Clojure's everything-is-a-map toolkit is that getters and setters are a waste of time. Clojure was built, in large part, in response to the crappy 2008 Java workflow, where you had to write getters, setters, and builders, and you took on all this bloat that nobody enjoyed.
The problem is that if you want to represent your data using the built-in defprotocol and defrecord, and you want to define functions that depend on the presence of a certain field, then the only way to encode that information into the protocol is to add getter and setter metohds to it. icky.
You can also use a combination of protocol + malli schema to represent this, but then when you use it, you need to specify 'this function takes as input something that both implements this protocol and implements this Malli schema'. Also icky.
What we want is something we can use in the style of defprotocol and defrecord, but gives us all the getters and setters and map-like stuff by default. The key insight is that if a field exists in a record, we get all the other good stuff, so we just need to add support for protocols with required keys.
Deft v0.2.0 adds support for namespaced keys in type and protocol definitions. i.e., you can now do:
(defp Positioned :required-keys [::pos - ::Point])
and
(deft Circle [::location/position radius])

(>Circle ::location/position [1 2] :radius 12)
this is useful because you can now define methods that depend on those fields being present i.e.:
(defp Gremlin :extends [location/Positioned])

(defmethod game-object/get-hitbox ::Gremlin [self]
  (js/Matter.Bodies.rectangle
   (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/x])
   (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/y])
   15 15))
Check it out!
https://github.com/sstraust/deft
How much LLMs is too much LLMs?
I finished reading On the Edge last week, and it was bad. Not that I don't respect Nate Silver. I respect him a lot. So when his seminal text on gambling and risk taking was a rambling mess, I was suprised and disappointed. Nevertheless, a completionist at heart, I trudged on, to the very end, where I was greeted with this message:
"ChatGPT was a significant help in writing this book, serving as a creative muse when coming up with things like chapter subheadings, metaphors, and analogies, and for refining my understanding of technical topics that are likely to be well represented in its corpus."
Technically he wrote the book by hand, and technically he typed the letters onto his keyboard, but you know, did he really? Did he put his whole thought and mind and being into every word on the page? Maybe. I'm reminded of the absolute classic [Simple Made Easy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SxdOUGdseq4), a video where so much of the core lecture is built on defining precise language, and saying exactly what you mean. When you offload that work, you don't just skip word choices, you skip that thinking, and you miss out on that organization and mental clarity.
In reading Nate's book, there's a real and noticeable difference between the language that feels baked into the organizational fabric of Nate's mentality, and the bits that were added on as an afterthought. The later chapters especially felt like they lacked that sort of mental compactification that cohesifies everything under one vision. I'm sad because this could have been a phenominal work, and it's clear that a lot of effort was made, especially into interviews and data collection, and it feels like it's just lacking that one last missing piece of insight to bring it all the way home.
So how much LLMs is too much LLMs? Well, when it comes to human connection, I'd say the answer is near zero. I don't want to read your AI generated e-mails, and I certainly don't want to read your AI generated essays. I'd much rather read your prompt instead, because I care about what you, yes, you personally think about, and I want to understand what you wanted to communicate.
Don't get me wrong, I love LLMs for the right purpose. I'd love to use LLMs on doctor's notes to build models that predict whether the flu is spreading. But when it comes to writing, especially this kind of writing, it just feels so unnecessary, because when you write down your thoughts, I already have exactly what I wanted, and it just feels so silly to add an extra stop in between.
As a poker player and game theorist, I'm sure Nate would appreciate the phrase "If you couldn't be bothered to write it, then I can't be bothered to read it". And you know, despite a belief that art can live separately from the artist, deep down for me this claim rings true. Not that the same words produced by a person are inherently different than the same words from an LLM, but it throws off my little Bayesian estimator a little.
If the smartest person I know spent 10,000 hours writing, editing, polishing, and publishing a 500 page novel, it tells me not just that the smartest person I know had some thoughts on a topic, but it tells me that they decided to spend 10,000 hours of their precious time, and of their precious energy to communicate this idea to me. It feels good that the time it took me to read it is porportional (and usually less than) the time it took you to write it, because it shows me that you care about the time and energy of creating this exchange.
And it's not just fully AI generated slop that hits this barrier. When you incorporate LLMs into your writing, even a little bit, you miss out on the ability to process your thoughts and create human connecti

Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak
Hannah Ritchie
Download
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.

The new Living Planet Index reports a 73% average decline in studied wildlife populations
Hannah Ritchie
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
OCTOBER 6
Child mortality has declined in all world regions
Max Roser
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
OCTOBER 1
Europe is older, but Latin America is aging faster
Esteban Ortiz-Ospina
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
SEPTEMBER 29
The United States is the world’s largest oil producer
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
When people think about global oil, their minds often go toward countries in the Middle East.
But it’s the United States that is the world’s largest oil producer.
The chart shows oil production by country since 1990. As you can see, the US has been the largest producer for the last nine years, since it overtook Saudi Arabia.
Production in the US gradually declined during the 1990s and early 2000s, then increased sharply after 2010 and is now at an all-time high.
This data comes from the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy.

title: AlphaNIST
content:
AlphaNIST
From AlphaGo to AlphaZero, reinforcement learning produced strategies that surprised expert players. AlphaZero learned from experience at scale, without human demonstrations.
AlphaNIST brings this philosophy to contact-rich, high-precision robotic assembly in simulation. An end-to-end policy learns how to complete the task, without prescribed manipulation stages.

The assembly challenge
NIST Assembly Task Board #1, shown fully assembled.
The NIST board has twenty assembly tasks, with parts as small as 4 mm. Fitting one part can take several changes of grasp and orientation. Tight clearances leave little room for error: a tilted nut can jam or cross-thread.
With several parts, the robot also has to choose an order. An installed component may block the gripper’s next move.
Robots can be creative—if we give them room.
Trying to prescribe every maneuver means anticipating how the robot should respond as contacts and obstructions change. A two-finger gripper may also need solutions quite different from those that come naturally to a human hand.
Perhaps the answer is to stop telling the robot how we think the task should be done, and let it learn how to get there. We give it a binary task reward for success and train it through vast amounts of diverse experience. That leaves room for the robot to discover solutions we might never have thought to teach.
How the robot learns
Experience diversity:
heterogeneous assets and initial states
One policy trains across twenty heterogeneous assemblies, starting from loose parts, in-hand grasps, and partial assemblies cached in simulation.
Near-complete starts let the robot practice finishing an assembly before it can solve the whole task. The cache supplies starting states, not demonstrations.

title: Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI - Apple
content:
PRESS RELEASE
October 13, 2026
Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI
A more capable and conversational Siri, faster performance, and an even more immersive home theater setup elevate the entertainment experience
The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, which transforms how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows; faster performance; and an even more immersive home theater experience.
CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the next generation of Apple TV 4K, delivering its most immersive home theater experience yet. The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, transforming how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows through a full-screen Siri AI experience.1 With built-in far-field microphones, Apple TV 4K also lets users talk to Siri completely hands-free.2
The new Apple TV 4K delivers even faster performance and, when paired with four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers, unlocks the most immersive home theater surround sound setup Apple has ever offered. As a home hub, Apple TV 4K also makes managing the smart home easier than ever, with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity descriptions and summarized notifications in the Home app, and control of accessories and scenes.3
The new Apple TV 4K can be pre-ordered starting today, with availability beginning November 13.
“The new Apple TV 4K is our most immersive home theater experience yet,” said Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, finding something to watch becomes a full-screen, conversational experience, and with built-in far-field microphones, it’s completely hands-free. Pair it with HomePod for the best surround sound setup we’ve ever offered, and it makes managing your Apple Home accessories easier than ever. Now, alongside HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection, it’s part of the most connected Apple Home we’ve ever built.”
An Entirely New Version of Siri Powered by Apple Intelligence
Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI to the living room with a rich, full-screen experience. An entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment. Users can simply ask Siri “What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” and see beautiful poster art pulled directly from the Apple TV app, along with relevant suggestions like “More award-winning comedies” to keep exploring. While watching, users can ask Siri AI follow-up questions and tap into Siri AI’s broad world knowledge to go deeper into a show, asking things like “Where was Pluribus filmed?” or “Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?” Responses appear in a compact, subtle overlay, providing helpful information when viewers ask while keeping them immersed in the action. With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, Siri AI on Apple TV 4K can now tap into a user’s personal context to answer requests like “Play the show Alinda recommended.”
A Fully Hands-Free Experience with Far-Field Microphones
The new Apple TV 4K features three far-field microphones, letting users control what they’re watching and discover new shows completely hands-free. Advanced echo cancellation intelligently isolates a user’s voice from background sound to deliver crystal-clear “Hey Siri” or “Siri” recognition, even while audio is playing.
Faster Performance, Smarter Remote
The A19 chip in the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance than the previous generation, for greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations. The A19 chip also includes a new, dedicated AV1 decoder, enabling more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth.
The new Siri Remote keeps its familiar design while adding Find My support with Precision Finding and an option to play a sound on the remote — making it far easier to locate.4
Apple’s Most Immersive Home Theater Ever
Pairing HomePod with Apple TV 4K already offers users an immersive viewing experience that’s easy to set up, and the new Apple TV 4K takes it even further. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. The four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space. HomePod (2nd generation) can also be used in this four-speaker setup for the ultimate audio experience, as long as the front and rear speaker pairs match.5
An Even Smarter Home Hub
The new Apple TV 4K continues to serve as a powerful home hub, giving users control of their smart home accessories from anywhere.6 With a compatible doorbell, notifications appear directly on the TV so users can see who’s at the door, speak with them, and control other accessories like unlocking the door — all without interrupting what they’re watching. Apple TV 4K supports automations, guest mode, and secure local processing of HomeKit Secure Video, now enhanced with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity video descriptions and summarized notifications. Users can also use Siri AI to control smart home accessories and turn scenes on or off hands-free. And with built-in Wi-Fi and Thread, Apple TV 4K can seamlessly connect and control a user’s smart home.
More Ways to Enjoy the Living Room
Apple TV 4K is more than just a way to watch — it’s a home essential that transforms the living room to reflect what users want in the moment. With Apple Fitness+, the living room becomes a workout studio, while Apple Arcade and the App Store’s library of games turn it into a home arcade. With the Apple TV app, users can stream hundreds of Apple Originals, including thrilling dramas, epic sci-fi, and feel-good comedies, as well as live sports such as Formula 1® in the U.S., Major League Soccer, and Friday Night Baseball.7 Users can also make FaceTime calls with Continuity Camera, view photos, and do even more, all from the big screen.8 With an iPhone or iPad, users can now customize how their iCloud photos appear on Apple TV, making it easy to set up personalized Memories & Slideshows or Portraits screen savers without making their entire library visible. Plus, a new screen saver shuffle feature automatically rotates between categories so there is always something new to see.
Private and Secure by Design
Like every Apple product, Apple TV 4K is designed with privacy and security in mind. Apple TV 4K and the A19 chip include Secure Exclaves: protected and compartmentalized runtimes used to process microphone data separately from the rest of the system. Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in the Secure Exclaves cannot be accessed by tvOS, apps, the user, or Apple.
Siri AI takes full advantage of the bold new architecture for Apple Intelligence. Siri requests on Apple TV 4K can use on-device processing or Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy of the device to the cloud. When processed in Private Cloud Compute, data is neither stored nor made accessible to Apple or anyone else. HomeKit Secure Video footage is stored end-to-end encrypted and never accessible to Apple.
Apple TV 4K and the Environment
Apple TV 4K was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. Apple TV 4K features 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed printed circuit boards, and 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets. The thermal module is made with 80 percent recycled aluminum, while the enclosure of the Siri Remote includes 100 percent recycled aluminum. Apple TV 4K meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based9 and designed to be recycled.
Pricing and Availability
Customers in the U.S. and 29 other countries and regions can pre-order Apple TV 4K (4th generation) starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app, with availability in stores beginning Friday, November 13.
Apple TV 4K (4th generation) is available for $299 (U.S.) or $49.83 (U.S.) per month for six months.10
Siri AI is available as a beta on Apple TV 4K (2nd generation or later), and is available at launch in the U.S., Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and the UK in English.
The new Siri Remote is compatible with Apple TV HD and Apple TV 4K, and is also available for purchase separately. Find My support is available on the Siri Remote (2nd generation or later).

title: PostEra - Machine Learning Researcher - Agentic Science
content:
Machine Learning Researcher - Agentic Science
RemoteMachine Learning /Full-Time /Remote
APPLY FOR THIS JOB
PostEra is building an AI-first biotech. We use Proton, our AI platform for medicinal chemistry, to accelerate the discovery of new medicines for patients. PostEra is advancing an internal pipeline focused on Women's Health and Fertility, and has used Proton to nominate multiple clinical candidates across PMOS and Fertility. PostEra also advances small molecule programs through partnerships with pharma. We've closed over $1B in AI partnerships including 4 multi-year agreements with Pfizer and Amgen. PostEra is also leading an antiviral drug discovery center for pandemic preparedness, funded by one of the largest grants in NIH history. 
PostEra's Organizational Structure
We believe time spent navigating complex hierarchies in organizations is better invested in the pursuit of novel technology and scientific discoveries. As such, our organizational structure is intentionally minimalist. 
We promote a culture where individual achievement is celebrated through proportional compensation and internal recognition, including meaningful promotions.
Ultimately, our collective focus is delivering cures to patients, which we believe needs a huge amount of cross-disciplinary collaboration, so we've fitted our organizational structure to serve that end.

Role Overview
In this role, you will develop the agentic research vertical at PostEra, using agentic systems to automate the development of mechanistic models for biochemical and physiological processes, and analyse biological data for target validation. You will interact closely with chemists and biologists to use these models to drive drug discovery decisions. 
You will also develop machine learning methods that can rapidly adapt to new drug discovery problems from limited labeled data. A particular focus is molecular and tabular in-context learning and building foundation models from PostEra’s proprietary multimodal data. You will build models that use the context of drug discovery effectively, determine which prior examples and tasks are relevant, quantify when transfer is helpful or harmful, and provide reliable predictions under distribution shift. 
You will help drive the full research loop: defining tasks, constructing datasets and evaluation episodes, developing strong baselines, training and scaling models, performing rigorous ablations, and translating successful methods into capabilities used by PostEra’s scientists. Prior drug discovery experience is not required, but you should be motivated to learn the domain and work closely with medicinal chemists, computational chemists, and other scientists.
Key Responsibilities
Agentic Research for Chemistry and Biology: Develop and benchmark agentic systems to automate the development of quantitative models to simulate biological and physiological processes, and the analysis of biological data. 
Research Direction and Execution: Independently identify, formulate, and lead research projects involving in-context learning, agentic systems, few-shot adaptation, tabular foundation models, and molecular machine learning.
In-Context Learning for Molecules: Design and train models that adapt to new assays, endpoints, targets, or chemical series using limited labeled context and heterogeneous historical data.
Benchmarking: Rigorously compare new approaches against strong baselines, curating test cases that deconfounds impact of different sources of bias. 
Cross-Functional Collaboration: Work with scientists to connect modeling objectives and evaluation metrics to practical decisions in potency modeling, ADME prediction, selectivity, lead optimization, and the design of early clinical studies.
Model Training and Scaling: Develop efficient training and data pipelines and, where appropriate, scale models across large collections of molecular and tabular tasks.
Research Engineering: Produce readable, reproducible research code; maintain well-tracked experiments; and contribute through code review, documentation, and shared modeling infrastructure.
Scientific Dissemination: Publish results in leading machine learning, medicinal chemistry, or computational biology venues. You will be an ambassador of PostEra to the scientific community. 
Key Requirements
PhD degree in machine learning, or STEM research involving the development of novel machine learning approaches 
Track record of high-quality research, such as publications and open-source contributions
Strong research or engineering experience in modern machine learning, deep learning, or statistical modeling, backed by understanding of the theory behind machine learning algorithms
Demonstrated expertise in at least one relevant area: agentic workflows for science, machine learning approaches to bioinformatics and clinical data modelling, in-context learning, tabular learning, few-shot learning
Hands-on experience training, debugging, and evaluating ML models in Python using frameworks such as PyTorch or JAX
Ability to independently translate ambiguous scientific or technical problems into well-defined ML projects, including datasets, task definitions, baselines, metrics, and validation schemes
Ability to design careful experiments, benchmarks, and ablations that distinguish improvements from biases, and understand which aspects of the model led to the improvements
Comfort working in a startup environment where priorities evolve, data is imperfect, and high-quality judgment matters as much as raw model complexity
Nice to Haves
Candidates are more likely to succeed in this role if they also have experience with one or more of the following:
Training tabular foundation models, particularly for sparse, heterogeneous, small-data, or high-missingness settings
Developing molecular in-context learning systems or adapting general-purpose in-context models to molecular or scientific data
Large model training, including 1B+ parameter models, distributed training, sharding, data parallelism, model parallelism, and large-scale data pipelines
The development of AI “co-scientist” systems for physical or biological problems 
Hands-on experience in modelling biological, biochemical or clinical data using machine learning approaches 
Moving research models into production scientific software or computational workflows
Salary: 200k - 300k

title: MIT class project turns into an FDA-cleared treatment for tremors | MIT News | Massachusetts Institute of Technology
content:
Wristband device from Encora Therapeutics started as a project in 2.009, MIT’s iconic product-design class.
Zach Winn | MIT News
Publication Date
October 2, 2026
PRESS INQUIRIES
Encora Therapeutics started as a class project in 2.009, in MIT’s iconic product-design class. The wearable is now an FDA-cleared treatment for tremors.
Credit: Courtesy of Encora Therapeutics
Previous image
Next image
In 2017, a man named Michael walked onto stage in front of a packed Kresge Auditorium at MIT and attempted to draw a spiral, a common test doctors use to diagnose Parkinson’s disease. His tremors, caused by the disease, made the exercise difficult. 
Then, Michael put on a wristband device made by a team of MIT students as part of 2.009 (Product Engineering Processes), who were presenting their prototype that evening.
Michael pressed a button and the device produced a subtle vibration. The vibration sent signals up his wrist and into his brain. His tremors dramatically decreased, and within seconds he was able to draw the spiral with much more precision, to a roaring ovation from the audience.
“When this device is turned on, I feel like I used to feel when I didn’t have Parkinson’s disease,” Michael told the crowd. “It’s an amazing, amazing feeling.”
The performance was so impressive that the student team received requests from classmates and others asking where they could buy the device for family and friends living with tremors. Unfortunately, the students had to explain there was only one — for the time being.
The event set off a near decade-long journey that began by leveraging MIT entrepreneurial resources like MIT Sandbox, MIT FUSE, and the MIT Venture Mentoring Service. In 2020, the student team turned into an official company, Encora Therapeutics. But there were still dozens of hardware iterations ahead. Then there were clinical trials. In one trial, 78 percent of patients reported benefits after 90 days of home use.
This February, nine years after Michael’s brave demonstration, all that work finally paid off: The FDA cleared Encora’s device to help adults with essential tremor, a condition similar to Parkinson’s that causes shaking, often in the hands. 
“It’s been a long and difficult — very difficult — journey, but also very rewarding, especially when we get feedback from patients,” says Daniel Carballo ’18, SM ’20, an Encora co-founder and vice president of strategy. “We hear stories from patients about how they’ve struggled with their condition and how much they benefit from this. It reminds us why we keep going.”
From classroom to commercialization
The three founders of Encora who are still with the company are Carballo, Allison Davanzo ’18, and Kyle Pina ’18. They were each seniors in 2017 when they enrolled in 2.009, MIT’s popular product-design class.
The semester began with a brainstorming session in which groups of about 17 students were asked to come up with dozens of potential product ideas. Carballo proposed a wearable device that used mechanical vibration to send signals to the brain to reduce tremors. The initial idea was to help patients with Parkinson’s disease.
“It was one of hundreds of throwaway ideas,” Carballo recalls. “The initial concept was inspired by classes I had taken in robotics around neural control of movement. I had a preliminary understanding of how an electromechanical device might interact with the body’s control systems and feedback loops that control movement to relieve pathological control of movement.”
The team eventually whittled their long list of ideas down to a few. Carballo’s idea was finally selected by a vote of 16-1 — with Carballo the only dissenting vote.
“I tried to explain to the team that this was so far-fetched that there was no way, in one semester, we would be able to make anything,” Carballo recalls. “Thankfully, I got outvoted.”
Through most of the semester, Carballo’s pessimism looked justified. At every class milestone, the team lagged behind other teams. Then, the week before final presentations, they met Michael, whose severe hand tremors were the result of early-onset Parkinson’s.
“He was a home renovator, so he worked with his hands, but his tremors had progressed to the point that he struggled to turn a screwdriver, use a drill, or even fill out paperwork,” Carballo recalls. “He had become reliant on his wife and daughter not only to run his business, but to help him with everyday activities.”
By this point, the 2.009 team had a prototype that would vibrate to send mechanical feedback to the brain. Carballo described it as “a foamcore box with a Raspberry Pi chip and some wires coming out.” When Michael put on the device and turned it on, his tremors dramatically decreased.
“It was like a light switch turned on and his tremors stopped,” Carballo says. “His wife and daughter started crying. A week later, he was gracious enough to repeat the process on stage for the final presentations.”
The presentation — and the outpouring of interest from people who wanted it for loved ones with Parkinson’s — made the team determined.
“It showed us there were a lot of people with this problem that could really benefit from this,” Carballo says. “A subset of the team became possessed. It would have been such a shame to know this could exist and to have it never leave the classroom.”
Some team members began using MIT’s entrepreneurial resources to commercialize the technology, initially focusing on Parkinson’s. They ran their first clinical trial with 20 Parkinson’s patients in 2022 in collaboration with MassGeneral Brigham. But they soon learned more patients are living with essential tremor.
“It was a greater unmet need,” Carballo says. “There are a lot of drugs being developed for Parkinson’s disease, but essential tremor hasn’t experienced that same innovation.”
Today scientists think tremor is caused by malfunctioning signals in the regions of the brain responsible for interpreting sensory input and coordinating movement.
“In these diseases, neurotransmitter deficiencies result in this pulsed signaling in the brain that manifests as tremors that are basically pulsed motor outputs,” Carballo says.
One current approach to target those signals is surgery that involves drilling holes in the skull to insert electrodes that drive new electrical patterns in the brain. Encora’s watch-like product targets the same brain regions with mechanical vibrations at the wrist.
“We’re applying mechanical stimulus, basically vibration, to stretch receptors in the wrist, which tell your body where it is in space,” Carballo explains. “The stimulation causes the receptors to activate and send a patterned signal to peripheral nerves of the wrist, that then carry the signal to the peripheral nervous system and into the central nervous system, to the same regions of the brain targeted by surgery.”
In 2024, Encora ran a randomized control trial with 47 patients living with essential tremor. Last year, the team ran a 59-person trial where patients used the devices at home. In both trials, more than 70 percent of patients experienced meaningful improvement.
The results were promising enough to gain what’s known as 510(k) clearance from the FDA for use as a medical device, in February of this year.
Helping patients
Most patients see rapid benefit when using Encora’s device. Patients have described the device as life-changing. Some say it allows them to do tasks they haven’t been able to do in years.
“We see some patients using the device 12, 14 hours a day,” Carballo says.
Today, Encora is focused on building a national sales force and working to secure coverage from insurers. As the company ramps up production, the product will finally become available for patients who qualify.
Further down the line, Encora hopes to fulfill its original mission of helping mitigate tremors in patients with Parkinson’s. Carballo believes the approach also holds promise for many other patients.
“There is a surprisingly long list of diseases that this could work for,” Carballo says.  “The most obvious are neurological movement disorders, but the bigger picture of wearable neuromodulation is a rapidly growing field that has seen therapeutic benefit across a broad range of diseases. We see this as a platform technology.”

title: Is ‘Attention’ the Essence of Intelligence? | Quanta Magazine
content:
QUALIA
Is ‘Attention’ the Essence of Intelligence?
A mathematical mechanism enables AI models to process language at scale, undergirding the current AI revolution. Our columnist asks: Why is attention the key?
7
Lisett Ledon for Quanta Magazine
Introduction
By
Natalie Wolchover
Columnist
October 12, 2026
VIEW PDF/PRINT MODE
artificial intelligence
computer science
large language models
mathematics
neural networks
Qualia
All topics
E
verything that’s swept the world since the 2022 release of ChatGPT — “the AI economy”; data centers; chatbots acting as best friends, doctors, and mathematicians; talk of existential risk — it all starts, in some sense, with an intern in a University of Montreal lab named Dzmitry Bahdanau.
It was 2014. The 23-year-old Belarusian, who had been coding competitively since he was a kid but hadn’t done academic research before, was asked to help figure out how to get a computer to translate sentences from English to French. Bahdanau was working with artificial neural networks, which had already shown promise in pattern-recognition tasks such as deciphering handwriting and identifying objects in photos. The networks learn to recognize patterns by strengthening and weakening connections between nodes in response to training data. Bahdanau quietly doubted their potential to achieve anything like human-level intelligence, but his adviser, the computer scientist Yoshua Bengio, and the postdoc on the project, Kyunghyun Cho, were believers. And translation was widely seen as a formidable and interesting problem for neural networks to try to solve.
In philosophy, “qualia” refers to the subjective qualities of our experience: what it’s like for Alice to see blue or for Bob to feel delighted. Qualia are “the ways things seem to us,” as the late philosopher Daniel Dennett put it. In these essays, our columnists follow their curiosity, and explore important but not necessarily answerable scientific questions.
Translation is not as simple as swapping each English word for a French one. Languages have different grammatical structures and are riddled with idioms and connotations, all of which had long stymied attempts to automate the process. You can’t simply implement rules of translation because there are none. But neural networks seemed promising because they learn by example. They can be trained on huge databases of paired English and French sentences to, eventually, absorb the quasi-rules, exceptions, and subtleties.
Results had been mediocre, though; the longer the sentence, the worse neural networks performed. That’s because researchers were trying to cram each sentence’s data into a fixed amount of memory before decoding the sentence in the target language. It was a bottleneck that limited how complex and sophisticated translations could be. The network architecture just wasn’t right.
So Bahdanau tried something different. “It was just obviously the right thing to do — one of these things that happens once in a while in science where it’s just very clear to someone who is not very experienced in the field,” he recalled, speaking to me from Montreal, where he still works in AI. “And it just worked. From the very first attempt.”
Bahdanau’s trick, a mathematical operation that he, Cho, and Bengio referred to as “attention,”  enabled their neural network to translate long sentences
(opens a new tab)
just as well as short ones. That meant the approach was scalable. Other AI researchers at the time quickly integrated attention into their neural network designs. Then, in 2017, a team at Google devised a new kind of neural network architecture called a transformer that supercharged the attention method and stripped away everything else. The team’s paper, “Attention Is All You Need
(opens a new tab)
,” reported that transformers achieved state-of-the-art translation while requiring a fraction of the computation needed to train prior models. The paper, which has since been cited more than 250,000 times, was a watershed moment in AI. Large language models such as ChatGPT and Claude followed.
Given the staggering power that’s been unleashed, it’s worth asking what this attention mechanism is exactly, why it is “all you need,” and why machine translation was the task that unlocked it all. Attention is a way for us to understand how a single AI model can converse with us, diagnose diseases, generate realistic videos, solve long-standing math problems, and more. Is it somehow at the heart of intelligence — artificial and otherwise?
Sentences with pronouns such as “it” in them illustrate the challenge that attention overcomes. Consider: “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.” And: “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too wide.” To translate these sentences correctly into French, an AI model must determine that, in the first one, “it” refers to the animal, which is a masculine word in French, so the translation should use that form of the pronoun, il. But in the second sentence, “it” refers to the street, a feminine word that requires a different pronoun, elle. How can the machine figure this out?
And it just worked. From the very first attempt.
Dzmitry Bahdanau
Bahdanau remembered doing translation exercises when he was learning English in school. To write each next word of his translated sentence, he’d have to glance all around the source text to figure out what should come next. “Literally you have your source sentence on the left and your writing on the right, and you’ll be, like, turning your head, left-right, left-right,” he said. “That process is what I expressed as a neural mechanism.” The tool of attention that he gave to his neural network was a mathematical way for the network to identify the word or words anywhere in a sentence that would most inform the next word of the translation. In the case of our ambiguous pronoun, “it,” the system navigates the rest of the sentence to determine which words affect its meaning the most.
A transformer consists of many layers of nodes connected to nodes in adjacent layers. When a sentence is fed into a transformer, each word is first converted into a numerical representation called a vector, which we can imagine as an arrow pointing in a certain direction. These vectors pass through the network, and numbers called weights (determined by the model’s training) dictate how they are transformed in each layer. The weights turn each word’s current vector representation into three new vectors specific to that word — a “query,” “key,” and “value” — that each serve a different purpose in the attention operation.
The network performs this operation several times in parallel through systems called attention heads. An attention head compares each word’s query with the keys of all the other words in the sentence. How well these vectors match up — how much they point in the same direction — determines how strongly the value of each other word contributes to a new, updated vector for the word at hand. Information about other words in the sentence literally becomes incorporated into each word’s representation. The system is converting context into math.
When “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired” enters a transformer, the first stack of layers in the network, known as the encoder, uses the attention operation to build up a contextual understanding of the sentence. In each layer, each attention head generates a query (along with a key and value) for “it.” This query vector can be thought of as a request for information that exists elsewhere in the sentence. For instance, in a deep layer (after the network has already accumulated information about words), the query for “it” might be interpretable as: “I need an earlier noun that could plausibly be the thing that is tired.” Meanwhile, the key associated with “animal” might effectively advertise itself as a noun that’s capable of being tired, among many other features. Its key therefore matches the query better than the key for “street.” And that causes the value associated with “animal” to contribute more heavily to the updated representation of “it.”
That new, context-enriched representation of “it” passes into the next layer. There, the network performs attention all over again. Successive rounds give the words increasingly rich representations of themselves.
Experts say it’s often hard to interpret what any given attention head is doing, but collectively they pick up on many kinds of relationships, from the partnership between nouns and verbs to the association between living beings and feelings. Later layers build on associations established by earlier layers, so that by the time the sentence emerges from the encoder, “it” is imbued with something resembling meaning.
After that, the second part of the transformer, the decoder, produces the French translation one word at a time, using attention to draw on the encoder’s numerical representations of the English words as it decides which French word to spit out next. The contextual information encoded in the English sentence helps translate “it” as the masculine il.
Crucially, no one had to tell a transformer that animals get tired and streets may be wide. The neural network discovers such associations during training, by learning from huge numbers of English sentences paired with their French translations. These associations get built into the weights. The network starts out with random weights that produce unhelpful queries, keys, and values, and thus poor translations. But each translation error sends a correction signal backward through the network that slightly alters the weights that produced it. Through trillions of these adjustments, the network eventually generates useful vectors that yield correct translations, even when it processes sentences it has never seen before.
Attention turned out to be the right mathematical operation for linking words and building context — the fundamentals of translation. And when you can translate blocks of text of unlimited size, it seems you can do anything.
A neural network that has learned enough about language to translate sentences from English into French can also complete sentences in either language. Predicting the next word of a translation is, in other words, a subtask of the more general task of “predicting the next word,” period. And that’s what large language models do. They’re trained on the contents of the entire internet, learning which words should attend to which other words in all sorts of contexts. They process and reprocess the whole dataset and try trillions of times to predict the next word in whatever part of the web they happen to be in at any point during training. The connections between neurons in these models are gradually tweaked in a way that produces patterns of attention between words that are ever more useful for predicting the next word in any context — or for producing an appropriate response to a prompt from a human.
From the ability to translate the word “it,” we somehow got a revolution.
“That’s quite a leap, isn’t it?” said Llion Jones, one of the authors of “Attention Is All You Need,” who is now the chief technology officer of Sakana AI.
Jones and others suspect that predicting the next word, which is known as language modeling, is “AI-complete”: a task so difficult that solving it means you have arguably solved AI in general. The reason it may be AI-complete is that this task includes, as a subtask, virtually anything humans do in written form. “The internet has translations,” Jones notes. “So if I said ‘“The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired” in French is [blank],’ then in order to complete that sentence, the transformer needs to be able to translate into French. If I say ‘2 + 3 is [blank],’ it needs to do arithmetic. If it sees a bunch of mathematical symbols in a row and wants to know what comes next, it needs to understand high-level mathematics. If I say ‘The president of the United States is [blank],’ it needs to know facts. So being able to predict the next word requires you to be able to do all these things. And because it’s AI-complete, language modeling is kind of the closest definition that we have to intelligence.”
The current paradigm won’t solve this [efficiency] problem. You seem to have to jump to something very, very different.
Llion Jones, Sakana AI
It might not be apt to say that an LLM “knows” or “understands” anything — not in the way that a human does — but that’s just how we’re accustomed to talking about the abilities they display. Regardless, attention is the tool by which artificial neural networks access and convey meaning, association, and context, often well enough to astonish us with their fluency. (For tasks such as advanced mathematics, today’s frontier AI models often have more explicit formal reasoning and proof verification systems layered on top of their language modeling to check their work.)
But what about human intelligence? Might our brains employ a mechanism similar to the mathematical operation Bahdanau invented? After all, we, too, do something akin to “producing the best possible next word” when we speak, write, and even think. Perhaps our form of intelligence is tantamount to language modeling, too?
Cognitive scientists have begun to study this question — a new version of the ancient question of how language relates to thought. To be sure, the success of LLMs shows how much information about the world is encoded in the statistical patterns of language alone. The question is: When we master language, does intelligence come for free?
RELATED:
Is AI the End of Math As We Know It?
Are We Thinking Correctly About AI Intelligence?
In a First, AI Models Analyze Language As Well As a Human Expert
Why Language Models Are So Hard To Understand
What the Most Essential Terms in AI Really Mean
Recent research
(opens a new tab)
persuades me that human thought is not purely linguistic (and most other animals’ intelligence is not linguistic at all): When we are thinking, more brain regions light up than just the specialized networks in the cerebral cortex that are associated with language. Language is how we communicate about the world, but our thoughts seem to draw on sensory impressions, physical and social experiences, memories, and reasoning abilities that exist at least partly outside the brain’s language networks. So language modeling seems to be merely a powerful component of human cognition, not its equivalent or source.
As for how we do “it” — how I instantly understand that it’s the animal rather than the street that is tired — no one yet knows. Jones, for his part, now thinks that attention is not all you need to truly master language modeling. After all, the brain evidently accomplishes this task far more efficiently than transformers do. content:
News
OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
Federal prosecutors say an employee from Saudi Arabia planted an audio recorder and left another unattended in his bag.
An OpenAI engineer concealed a recording device in a conference room used by executives at the company, the Department of Justice claims. |
Source:
Justin Katigbak/The Standard
By George Kelly and Michael McLaughlin
Share
1
There are 1 comments on this story
Published Oct. 13, 2026at1:17pm
Updated Oct. 13, 2026at1:44pm
An OpenAI engineer has been arrested on suspicion of hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday and remains in custody.
An unattended bag found in the company’s offices contained Alfozan’s wallet and identification, as well as a recording device, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in San Francisco.
ADVERTISEMENT
Alfozan has worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors said.
OpenAI personnel found the device Sept. 30. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and had been concealed in toilet paper, the complaint says. The company determined it was installed around Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted.

title: Frontier Models for Every Robot: Announcing our API beta
content:
Physical Intelligence (π)
Home
Research

Frontier Models for Every Robot
Announcing our API beta
Published
October 13, 2026
We are making our latest models available for training and inference through the Pi API beta.
Deploying robots is challenging. Besides identifying the right use case and building the right hardware, developers need models intelligent enough to perform the task at hand. General-purpose robotic foundation models such as π0 and π0.5 offer a promising way to tackle this challenge. They provide a strong foundation of physical knowledge and capabilities, substantially reducing the data and effort needed to adapt to new tasks, environments, or robots. But adapting them still requires ML infrastructure, compute, and complex data pipelines, which are difficult in their own right. What if the latest and most powerful robotic foundation models could be adapted to each application through a simple and ready-made API?
The Pi API does that for you. You upload data, launch fine-tuning on compute and infrastructure we manage, and access fine-tuned models via a hosted gateway to run inference. The latest model available through the API already provides more data-efficient fine-tuning and improved capability for our partners. Since Pi can update the models underpinning the API rapidly, we plan to continue enabling access to our latest and most capable models. Launching the beta is our first step in providing the physical intelligence foundation the community can build upon and enabling end-to-end autonomy.
To ensure that the API supports diverse applications, we sought to answer two key questions. First, do our models support a broad range of applications and robotic hardware in diverse industries? Second, how easily does the API enable developers to iterate toward useful, practical autonomy?
Supporting a broad range of applications in diverse industries
To discover how broadly our models can adapt, we work closely with companies deploying robots to build autonomy systems for their applications. These collaborations let us validate how well our models perform across different tasks, hardware, and operating environments.

Across these initial collaborations, a common pattern emerged. The challenges differ from task to task: an inside-out garment, an ingredient that wouldn’t stay in a scoop, a manufacturing part that landed in the wrong position. But the process for improving performance was much the same: collect demonstrations, train a model, test it on the robot, and use the failures to decide what data to collect next. We built the API to let developers run this iteration loop themselves, using our latest models.
API workflow: Upload your data, fine-tune a π model, and run it on your robot through hosted inference. Use evaluation data to guide the next iteration.
We gave a small number of companies early access to the API to test whether they could improve autonomy on their own. We were impressed by how quickly they got started and began making progress. Their experiences offer a glimpse of what you could do with your own robots and data.

Most applications shown above, from Japan to Switzerland to deployments across the United States, ran with cloud-hosted inference through the API. These early deployments spanned a range of environments and tasks and highlighted areas for improvement, including network connectivity challenges for some.
Improving from feedback
The more our models are used, the more we learn how to improve them: by understanding the potential and limitations of our current models in real-world applications, we can make the next generation of models more broadly applicable, and make tangible progress toward truly general physical intelligence. But the range of real-world tasks is enormous, and understanding the broad range of tasks that robots could do requires making our models available for these tasks. Real-world robotic applications are not easy: tackling robotic construction, robotic surgery, or warehouse automation each requires an entire company. If each such application requires solving the physical intelligence problem from scratch, the challenges become insurmountable. By making our models available through the API, we accelerate the growth of the robotics ecosystem and, in the process, advance our own understanding of physical intelligence.
The examples above show that the models we develop can be used for real, useful applications, and that our partners are able to use the API to independently iterate on policies and improve autonomy on their tasks. We’re still early, and feedback from developers will help shape future releases.
If you would like to participate in the beta, please tell us what you want to build.

Minions: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices
Authors
Jianhua Li, Yun Xing, Girisha De Silva, Ryan Flint, Kai Yuan, Sean Suchter
View publication
Copy Bibtex
The increasing demand for GPU-accelerated machine learning inference has exposed limitations in centralized GPU infrastructures, including high cost, limited elasticity, and long wait times under resource constraints. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon–based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Minions enables teams to leverage existing hardware without requiring additional GPU procurement. The system provides flexible GPU inference task execution, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilization. Our experience shows that idle macOS devices can be transformed into a practical distributed GPU inference platform in environments where centralized GPU resources are constrained.

title: The Universe of Discourse : Maybe a better way to track the release history of a Git repo
content:
The Universe of Discourse









Tue, 06 Oct 2026
Maybe a better way to track the release history of a Git repo
While I was still at ZipRecruiter, our Git monorepo was developing an annoying problem: it had too many refs.
Whenever there was a deployment of any of the applications in the repo, to staging or to production, the deployment tool would create a tag object with a name like this:
refs/release/stg.www.our-app-2019-09-06T114410.954-0700-treesha-179dab6fd11bee5195f0f8e31cea3edfb86ae23b
The tag contained the name of the target tier of the deployment (stg here, for “staging”), the app name and class of hosts on which it ran, www.our-app in this case, the date and time, and the hash of the tree that was deployed. This made a complete record of what was deployed, where, and when.
After we had been doing this for a while, there were thousands of these tag objects. Git is well-designed for handling thousands of commits, but not for handling thousands of refs. Perhaps this has changed, but at the time, Git would store refs in a file called packed-refs, which, for each ref, contained an entry with the ref's name and the ID of the object to which it referred.
(As with all things Git, the actual situation is somewhat more complicated. These additional ramifications don't affect the following discussion.)
Any operation that required resolving a ref name to its object had to search through the packed-refs file, which was taking an appreciable amount of time, far more than was desirable for an operation that everyone did many times a day. This affected not just local operations but operations on the Git server as well, and it was clear that it was only going to get slower as time went on. Also, the outputs of commands like git fetch and git branch were becoming increasingly cluttered with the names of tag objects whose only purpose was to record release history.
It seemed reasonable to me record the deployment history in the repository, but using thousands of tag objects clearly had serious drawbacks. In addition to the performance problems, the metadata itself was purely a convention in the tag name format, not legible to Git itself. There was a tree ID there, but nothing enforcing the rule that the tag should refer to a commit with that tree.
Also, the tag objects themselves seemed poorly-designed for the purpose. One good reason for storing history data in the respoitory is to render it immutable. But tags aren't immutable! They can be deleted and new ones can be inserted at any time, with any names desired.
And more important: consider the most natural sort of question that someone might want answered by the release history:
When did we last deploy the www.our-app app to production?
The only way to answer this question was to get the full list of all tags, filter it for prod.www.our-app, then sort by date and take the last item.
Or similarly: What if the most recent staging deployment had turned out to be bad, and we wanted to immediately revert to the version before that? Again, we (or the reversion process) would have had to filter and sort a list of thousands of tags, then pick out the second-last one.
I proposed this alternative in 2019. It stores the deployment history of each app as a series of unnamed but related Git objects, using Git's own history mechanism, so it's simple, efficient, and meshes well with Git's commands.
I don't think it was ever adopted, and it might turn out to have serious drawbacks I haven't foreseen. But it might be useful to someone in a similar situation.
Maintaining an audit and reversion trail without thousands of refs
Currently, each time a new version of an app is deployed, we create a ref:
refs/release/stg.www.our-app-2019-09-06T114410.954-0700-treesha-179dab6fd11bee5195f0f8e31cea3edfb86ae23b
As these refs proliferate, many operations in the Git repo become slower and slower.
We can record this information in a way that is at least as useful and which doesn't clutter up the ref list.
Current practice
At present, the release procedure creates a ref something like this:
A new release is created at commit H
A new tag object is created, pointing to H, something like
git tag -a refs/release/stg.www.our-app-2019-09-.... H
Every new tag object has a name in the ref database. This adds a name for every release. The structure is something like this:
One ref object per release, each pointing to its own head commit
Alternative proposal
Each (tier, app) pair is represented by a linked list of release commits
The head of the list is the most recent release
One ref points to the head of the list
Older releases can be found by following the links back in time
Main point of this proposal: There is only one ref for each (tier, app) pair, no matter how many releases have been done.
It will look like this:
A chain of metainfo commits, each with the previous metainfo commit as first parent and the actual release commit as second parent
The one ref (which might or might not be an actual ref object) is named stg.www.our-app. That points not to the actual release commit, but to a commit that contains metainformation, such as the treesha. The metainformation could be stored in any of several ways. (See below.) The exact time of the release doesn't need to be stored explicitly because it is exactly the time at which the metainfo commit was created.
The metainfo commit has two parent commits. One is the actual release commit, the one that, in the current system, is the target of the named ref object. The other parent is the metainfo commit from the previous release.
The metainfo commits are chained together exactly the same way Git normally chains commit history, so the usual Git commands will work on the release history in reasonable and useful ways. In particular, the command git log stg.www.our-app will produce a listing of the release history.
Technical details
Creating this sort of two-parent commit is easy. Suppose the ref stg.www.our-app points to the current metainfo commit. And suppose we want to release new commit H. We do:
(Write some useful commit message into /tmp/message.$$.)
git commit-tree -p refs/release/stg.www.our-app -p H \
    H^{tree} < /tmp/message.$$
This creates a new metainfo commit with two parents, given by the arguments of the -p options. The first parent is the metainfo commit for the current release and the second is new commit H.
The git commit-tree command creates the new metainfo commit and writes its SHA on standard output. Say this SHA is N.
git push origin N:refs/release/stg.www.our-app
The release ref now points to the metainfo commit for the new release.
Usage
This will be easier to use than what we have now, because Git's command set was designed to manage a list of commits linked in this way; this is exactly how Git normally expects to represent history. This natural fit with Git's command set shows up in many places.
You can fetch a complete release history for any project with a single fetch:
git fetch origin refs/release/stg.www.our-app:HISTORY
After this, git log HISTORY will list the entire release history in reverse chronological order. All the usual git-log options make sense to filter or search this list. For example, if we want to find the last release before a certain date, we can use:
git log -1 --until=date HISTORY
If we want a forward-chronological list of release commit SHAs with their release dates, we could use something like:
    git log --reverse --format="%P %cd" HISTORY
At all times:
The current release commit is accessible at HISTORY^2.
The metainfo commit from n releases ago is at HISTORY~n.
The release commit from n releases ago is at HISTORY~n^2.
Notice: if M is a metainfo commit that describes a release, M^ is the metainfo commit for the release before that, and M^{2} is the exact commit that was actually released. We don't have to record the tree IDs in the ref names; the tree that was released in release M is M^{2}^{tree}. These notations will work as expected in all git commands; see git-rev-parse.
Because Git naturally understands this way of organizing history, it will be easy to locate a particular previous release for rollback. When we roll back, we can roll back to the exact same commit as before: the new metainfo commit and the old one can share the exact same release commit object.
We can see the differences between the last two releases, without knowing their exact dates, with something like:
    git diff HISTORY~1^2 HISTORY^2
The metainfo commit is a full commit with a full set of Git commit metadata, such as a creation date. It has a commit message where we can record any unstructured text that we want. We could also require the commit message to be in TOML format, or we could use the tooling provided by Git to store semi-structured information in the commit message; see git-interpret-trailers.
If the built-in commit structure is not big enough for everything we want to record, the metainfo commit also has an associated tree where we could record any amount of structured information. In the example above I had its tree be identical to the release commit's tree, which might be convenient. (That way, if you wanted to see the files that were released, you could look in either the release commit or the metainfo commit; this would make some of the commands simpler.) But the tree doesn't have to be the same. We could also add metainformation files to this tree, or we could commit an entirely unrelated tree with nothing in it other than structured metainformation.
Performance?
Ploni Almoni asks about the performance issues of tracing out a linked list of commits. But this is exactly the same mechanism that Git normally uses to record history. When we do git log, Git is tracing a linked list of commits in exactly the way suggested here. If any operation in Git is going to be fast, it will be this one.
Git currently takes a few seconds to trace the 275,000-commit history of our monorepo. Tracing the similarly-structured history of a few hundred release commits is not going to be an issue.
I wrote this originally, but my only copy was in the form of a PDF. I had Claude convert the PDF to Markdown, which is the native format accepted by my blog, and the two diagrams to SVG. I then substantially edited the text and the diagrams. Along the way Claude pointed out three minor errors, which I corrected. I also took Claude's advice on how to adjust the colors from the original to make them more legible to color-blind readers.
Every word was written by my brain using my fingers.
