title: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
content:
The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
2 days ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Madison Chapman
Alexander Pomper
(Credit: Alexander Pomper)
Trevor Warmedahl has spent years documenting rare and traditional cheesemaking methods, and believes that "cheese is an edible manifestation of a place".
Trevor Warmedahl was working as a commercial cheesemaker in Seattle when he realised he was using milk that came from animals he never saw. So, he quit his job and set off on what has become a global odyssey to discover places that still make cheese the old-fashioned way. 
In 2019 he arrived in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and lived alone in a yurt with a dog as his companion. He soon discovered that dairy was sacred there: the women flicked milk into the air before cheesemaking, a gesture of respect called a milk libation. He visited homes where whey bubbled over central hearths and fresh, unripened byaslag cheese covered tables. After hiking to shrines, he noticed people offered dairy products as a symbol of purity.
As summer unfolded and city-dwellers migrated to the Mongolian steppe to farm, Warmedahl itched to join. He jumped on a Soviet-era coal-powered sleeper train for a rickety overnight ride across the Gobi Desert. On the journey back to Ulaanbaatar, he met a local who invited him to stay with her herder family on the Zavkhan grassland.
Trevor Warmedahl
Warmedahl spent time living in rural Mongolia and milking yaks (Credit: Trevor Warmedahl)
ADVERTISEMENT
Warmedahl spent that summer waking before dawn to milk yaks, chasing livestock up the valley on horses, listening to shepherds' folk songs at sunset and cooking milk into dehydrated, sweet-and-sour curds called aaruul. The experience inspired him to seek out other places preserving rare cheesemaking traditions before they disappeared.
During the past six years, Warmedahl has hitched, hiked and driven through more than 20 countries, documenting traditional cheesemaking and pastoral lifestyles, and offering workshops on natural dairy processing. After recently completing a 193km (120-mile) cheese trek across the Peaks of the Balkans Trail, he shared with the BBC what cheesemaking reveals about a place.
You've been to so many places – Bulgaria, Pakistan, Italy, Austria, Cambodia. Share a standout adventure. 
Ancestral cheeses in Georgia have no analogues – I call them "fossil cheeses" because they were almost lost but are making a comeback as part of a broader post-Soviet cultural revival. My pinnacle moment happened in Tusheti, a mountain region bordering Russia near the tourist village of Omalo.
The cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness
I showed up with vague directions to the shepherds' summer camp, which was deep in the valley. That's a theme: the cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness. It was drop-dead gorgeous, just me and my backpack. The valley ends on an abrupt cliff, with deteriorating medieval stone towers. Shepherds build their camps from the decay. I saw how these guys milked sheep by hand with wooden pails, rustic-style. It's a feta-like cheese called Tushuri guda, aged in inside-out sheepskins. At the end of the season, I walked about 130km (81 miles) back down the valley with them and 300 sheep. The herd has done this for generations – they know where to go. The shepherds just coordinated, and it created this crazy lawless feeling with dogs barking and me, chasing stray sheep down ravines.
Trevor Warmedahl
Warmedahl lived and worked in Tusheti, Georgia with shepherds (Credit: Trevor Warmedahl)
At night we'd build a campfire and drink, and even with the language barrier, we'd relate through food. Sometimes language isn't needed. In cheesemaking, if two hearts want to connect, they'll find a way.
How is cheese and cheesemaking a reflection of a community's history and culture? 
Cheese is a sensory experience and embodies larger ideas about how we live. It represents how meaningful human cultures can be. At its best, cheese reflects this complex relationship between humans, landscapes, microbial life and livestock at a time [when] we've become so separate from how food is made. And the cultural element holds the constellation together. 
Don't try something once, try it 10 times
The cheeses I highlight represent an older mentality, with a sense of stewardship over the places we live and farm. So, a little bit more of the wildness of nature slips into the product. [Cheese is] an edible manifestation of place, of cultural history transformed into delicious food. 
Why is cheesemaking especially important today? 
The diversity and range of cheese is infinite. When animals eat, they transform grass and entire landscapes into milk that becomes cheese, and animals can graze [almost] anywhere. So, it's a lifestyle that can move in response to climate uncertainty and desertification – real challenges today.
The cheeses I focus on – natural farmstead cheeses [made exclusively with milk from a farmer's own animals] – reflect deep, ethical relationships between people and livestock and highlight the incredible diversity of heritage livestock. With industrialisation, that diversity is vanishing at an alarming rate. So pastoral cheesemaking strikes me as profoundly sustainable.
Trevor Warmedahl
"Don't try something once, try it 10 times" (Credit: Trevor Warmedahl)
What can so-called "exotic cheeses" that challenge us reveal about a place? 
There's this greyish-brown cheese from Norway, gammelost, [covered in] moulds like fruit rot. It tastes like a musty cellar with bold, mouth-numbing spiciness. It wasn't for me. But deliciousness is cultural. It's taught. So, I always say: don't try something once, try it 10 times. Uncomfortable foods open doors. But be sure to eat them because you're interested in the culture, not because they're freaky to you.
One of the easiest ways to express interest in a culture is to say: feed me what you eat. When people realise you're genuine, the relationship deepens and you begin to understand their history through food. Funky cheeses become cultural emblems because of how obscure and special they are.
You set out on your global cheese journey without a real plan. What did this approach add to your experience?
Back then [in 2019], I was hopping on a whim from one volunteer gig to the next, drawn to remote places where people worked to protect and revitalise traditional cheeses. Workaway on farms, or staying for a while at guesthouses where cheese is made, are still amazing ways to go beyond tourism to see how people really live.
Cheese gives you access to a global community, like at [the Slow Food Cheese Festival in] Bra, Italy. But anything you can do to find that deeper experience – food, handicrafts – is worth it, even if you can't always plan in advance. If your heart is in the right place and you jump fully into adventure when it calls, the details will almost always work themselves out.  
Trevor Warmedahl
Warmedahl encourages responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism (Credit: Trevor Warmedahl)
What advice would you give fellow travellers about how to best experience unique cheeses abroad?
Find the cheese shop or cheesemonger that has the most local tilt and ask them which cheesemakers you can and should visit. Organising it yourself is cheaper. But there are also paid tours where you can experience a range of cheeses in a short period and really get to know a place. Just make sure that the cost actually supports local producers – that's what I call responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism.
How can other travellers seek out responsible agrotourism experiences?
Look for local cheesemakers and guides. It's also important to not expect farmers to sanitise things. It's normal to go to a farm and see broken-down equipment and mud. When we romanticise tradition, it encourages locals to put themselves in a museum. But tools [and] tradition have always evolved.

• Is cheese the new reason to travel?
• The woman saving Georgia's lost cheeses
We need to be open to the fact that it's not all grandmas spinning wool on wheels outside stone cottages. Then it becomes kind of a show, and we're pushing farmers to become something they're not for tourists. 
What places have exciting, overlooked, or under-the-radar cheeses? Where are you keen to travel next?
Hands down, Turkey. It's a universe of cheese that doesn't get enough attention. Tulum peyniri is emblematic of pastoral lifestyles and the extreme sacrifice at the root of dairying and – I'd argue – life. That's because it's aged mainly in furry goatskins, so it looks insane because it can take on animal shapes. Somehow, I didn't think it would be delicious. How good can goatskin-aged cheese be, right? It was phenomenal. I was blown away by deep flavours and textures I'd never seen in cheese before.
Alamy
Tulum peyniri is a Turkish cheese that's aged in furry goatskins (Credit: Alamy)
Turkish cheese needs to be talked about alongside Western Europe. More remote places have just as many fascinating cheeses to preserve and celebrate.

an update on character.ai
Today, we’re sharing that Character.ai has initiated a voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy process to facilitate a court-supervised sale of the company. 
Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. After a comprehensive review of our available alternatives, our board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides us with the best opportunity to maximize value for all of our stakeholders. 
We hope that the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.ai platform. If such a bid is unavailable, however, the platform will be wound down. 
As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority. 
What This Means for Our Community
The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time. 
We know that this news may raise questions for some of you. To learn more, please see our FAQs below. And if you need support, you can find helpful resources here.
1. Why did Character.ai file for Chapter 11?
Over the past year, we have taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds.  
 After a comprehensive review of available options, we determined the best path forward was to begin a Chapter 11 case to pursue a court-supervised sale of all or substantially all of our assets. We believe that this court-supervised process both maximizes the value of our business and provides the best opportunity for continued service to our platform users.
2. How long is the sale process expected to take?
We currently expect that the court-supervised sale process will be complete by the end of November or perhaps early December 2026.
3. What does this mean for users? 
The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time. We're focused on finding the best path forward for our platform and community.
4. Is my paid subscription still active?
Yes, your subscriptions remain active, and billing is unchanged for now. If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance.
5. What happens to user data and chats?
Your information continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy, and our data privacy and security practices are unchanged. As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website. 
To learn more, you can read the full press release HERE. Court filings and additional information relating to Character.ai’s Chapter 11 case can be found HERE, a website administered by Character.ai’s claims and noticing agent, Stretto, Inc.

title: Do Frameworks Matter Anymore?
content:
Home
2026-09-16
Do Frameworks Matter Anymore?
I'm not trying to be facetious. I really want consider whether or not, in 2026, in the age of vibe coding, agentic programming, loop or graph or whatever diagrammatic metaphor-based engineering is most popular, does it matters what web framework you use? More importantly (to me and my particular interests), and at the risk of Betteridge-ing myself: should we make new frameworks?
React won, so do we ever try anything new?
Is there now just more room for niches? Nobody cares about the implementation details. Nobody cares what's in a .tsx file. Does that open up new opportunities to try something new, or, since it doesn't matter, does the industry as a whole just decide to use the most stable thing, forever?
In this time of great disruption, we get the opportunity to rethink best practices (or in Remix's case, re-rethink), and lay everything on the table again. That doesn't mean everything stays on the table, just that we'll take the good, leave the bad, and modify the ugly. The question of this article isn't one that needs refuting, it's one worth considering seriously.
As someone who has worked on open source frameworks in a full-time capacity for 3 years, I'm deeply interested in this question. I'm not interested in protecting myself/my craft, I'm interested in bettering my craft and having a good career. I am considering and also trying to predict (and make) the future. It's humbling to remember "I could be wrong", and it's encouraging to remember most everyone else will be.
In this article, I want to break the question and its implications down into their more fundamental elements, so I can rebuild a version of reality worth pursuing and building. To do that, it would be worth first considering what a web framework is. I find this really hard, since it's a very nebulous and general term, and you end up comparing Flask to jQuery to React to Next.js. Instead, I think it's more helpful to consider what value frameworks provide. I think this statement is sufficient:
Frameworks provide abstractions, structure, and constraints for building your website.
Imagine
Imagine there's no React
It's easy if you try
No Svelte below us
Above us, only bi(nary)
Imagine all the people
Prompting for today
(Sorry, Svelte, for replacing you with the word "hell". It's not because I perceive a resemblance, I just liked the way it sounded.)
So let's return to the argument, and spell it out a bit more. This is the conventional wisdom I am hearing right now:
Since the models got good (circa Winter '25-'26) for agentic programming, I care less and less about the code (and you should too). This is particularly true with any frontend code, because it's all largely presentational. Therefore, if it looks good, it is good.

Given the state of the models, and given that React is already the most dominant UI framework, with the very popular meta-framework Next.js (plus a few other good choices like React Router and TanStack Start), there really is no need or value in trying anything else out. Plus, because there is vastly more React code out there in the wild, the models are trained more heavily on it and are therefore better (or at least more familiar) with React. The React singularity has already happened, accept it.
Obviously (I hope) I am now being a bit facetious. The argument is still worth considering, mostly because I see people cargo culting this opinion and React along with it into their vibe-coded apps. There are, however, some much more serious folks such as the Cursor team who do seem to be convinced that in the age of agentic programming using React is an advantage.
I'm tempted to dig into each of these claims:
You don't need to worry about frontend code
Models are best with React because of their training data
Models would be bad with a new framework because of a lack of training data
I'm not actually sure of the value, though, particularly in arguing about React. I have a much bigger issue with the logic, and it stems from my original question: Do frameworks matter anymore?
Here's what I don't get about the argument: why React? Why any framework or UI library at all?
If LLMs have gotten so good at frontend code, and if people care less and less about the details of their HTML, JavaScript, and CSS and only care that it looks and behaves properly, then why even put a layer of abstraction between the LLM and the website? If ever there were a time to embrace Web Components, surely it's now.
React no longer has to be one's personality. Disclaimer: I say this as someone with a YouTube channel named "React Tips with Brooks Lybrand". Plus, we already have AI labs to make our new personality, so we'll be fine.
Let me pitch the argument differently:
Since the models got good (circa Winter '25-'26) for agentic programming, it's easier than ever to build a beautiful and interactive website without having to worry about what we previously called DX (Developer Experience). My agent doesn't care about things like file-based routing, and why should I bother it with properly setting up a useEffect?

Plus, models are really well trained on JavaScript, HTML, and CSS (sort of), so there's really no need or value in adding any more layers of complexity.
I think there are some logical leaps and mistakes in this sentiment, but no more than in the first, more widely accepted one.
Either:
Frameworks do not matter, in which case you have no reason to use React.
You are likely still at an advantage using React, in which case frameworks do matter.
What is the value of a web framework?
Ah, the web framework. Where does it start, where does it end? What's its purpose? Do we even need any at all? After all, what was so bad about jQuery? Has anyone made the argument yet that we should just let the agent use jQuery since it's well represented in its training data? If not, they should. An agent doesn't care about spaghetti code, right?
I'm old enough to remember the "framework wars" of the 2010s. When I did my own evaluation for my company at the time, I was picking between React, Angular, and Vue. Those were the "frameworks" we talked about. Gatsby existed, but wasn't general-purpose enough (static-site generation only). Next.js was pretty cool, but also pretty limited (no good mutation story). For the most part, if you were in the React ecosystem, you just used create-react-app (CRA) and maybe you ejected if you actually had someone on your team who thought SSR was valuable and wanted to set it up.
I ultimately picked React, and many other people did too. But why? What made React so compelling as a framework?
If you ask the React team why React won or why it's so great, they will likely say "composition". I find it very difficult to encapsulate exactly what made React so special, but I think this is a big part of it. I didn't really understand what "composition" meant early in my career and React usage. I just knew that:
React was really easy to plug into an existing site
React had a really nice way to encapsulate logic and markup into contained and potentially reusable components
React had a robust and constantly growing ecosystem of libraries that helped fill in additional pieces I needed: routing, styling, head/meta tag management, etc.
I would learn later that React also provided server-side rendering (SSR) out the gate, making it look and feel a good bit like PHP with its HTML-in-your-scripting-language sort of experience. Setting this up was a bit more involved, especially for folks like myself who were more frontend-focused. This led to the rise of the "backend-for-frontend engineer" and the meta-frameworks like Next.js and Remix (the old one, sorry).
React was solving a number of problems. Despite what Mr. Rauch thinks (and ordinarily, he is pretty much on the money), React didn't "win" because it came with a component library that wraps a great style system and lower-level accessible components and utilities that you can own and morph to your own needs. shadcn/ui is awesome, don't get me wrong. But even within the component-library/design system story, it's the latest evolution in a long line of successors from Radix to Reach UI to Material UI to Bootstrap and many, many more that I'm skipping, forgetting, or unaware of. The existence of shadcn/ui on top of many other popular incumbents is a testament to what makes React great, not the other way around.
This long but brief diversion of why React "won" hardly does justice to the full history, and it certainly doesn't even touch on what makes other web frameworks interesting. Despite React's predominance, plenty of other frameworks and meta-frameworks get millions of weekly downloads and are loved by many a developer. It also completely glosses over the popularity of non-JavaScript-based frameworks such as Laravel and Ruby on Rails.
I don't know a better way to consider value frameworks provide without introspecting what made my first love, React, so special to me. React made it easier to build dynamic websites without ending up with spaghetti code, and spaghetti code was bad because it was costly to change and maintain in the long term. React enabled me, elevated me as an engineer, solved problems I didn't want to solve, and opened me up to an ecosystem of other developers who were making it better and building more useful tools on top of it.
As I stated at the top of this post, I think the value-add of a framework is pretty simple: frameworks provide abstractions, structure, and constraints for building your website.
This isn't even really a unique property of frameworks, this is true for all libraries, modules, classes, and functions. Code is a series of abstractions that express meaning and intent to computers and anything else that will manipulate or learn from that code. Previously, that meant humans, and we called it "reading the code", and so we cared a lot about things like variable names. These days the level of detail we care about is shifting and resettling. Maybe we're on some infinite curve and we'll care less and less about the trees until we don't even care about the forest. Personally, I'm doubtful, but I could definitely be wrong.
Either way, I think I still want a framework. I want code that's well tested, secure, easy to reason about, and that gets my agent in the grooves it needs to be in to produce results I like.
Everyone uses a framework
Alright, the jig is up, I'm being a little facetious when I ask "Do frameworks matter anymore?"
I recall that during a Q&A with the Core Team at React Conf 2024, Ricky Hanlon made this point:
You're either using a framework, or building a framework, and building a framework is really hard.
This wasn't the first time I'd heard this. In fact, at a prior job as an engineer on the web platform team of a Texas grocery store, we ran into the same thing. We built our own meta-framework around React to handle server-side rendering for initial requests, after which the application would hydrate the whole document and hand off routing on the client using React Router (v5?).
While we did have a cute name for this little meta-framework we made (exo, I believe, and no one could agree why it was called that), most engineers didn't think of it as a framework. I blame that mostly on the combination of a lack of features and a lack of marketing (why would we market an internal framework?). Nevertheless, we had still built our own framework, and it came with a lot of maintenance cost and burden, plus very few engineers actually understood how it worked, making it a pretty decent-sized liability.
Long story short, they started the process of moving off of this home-grown meta-framework and switching to Next.js. I didn't get to see the transition through because this was around the time I went to work with the Remix team at Shopify (of course we "joked" that it was this decision that drove me away).
The timeline of this anecdote is pretty definitively right before agentic programming would git gud. Assuming you're starting a greenfield project right now, and assuming it's not just for demonstration purposes or a 1-off presentational website, I think Ricky's statement is both more true now than ever, and a little bit wrong.
Let's start with the wrong: "building a framework is really hard". It's really not anymore. I mean, it depends on what you want. If you want a good, robust, bug-free, secure, full-stack framework, it's gonna take a lot more than a couple of prompts to really flesh out. And then when you start using it, you may find that LLMs can't really make it work for all the things you ask it to do, so they just quietly build hacks around your framework, and depending on how you're building this framework those hacks end up becoming part of the framework. Avoiding bolting on hacky workarounds and deciding on good, robust, and extensible abstractions require a bit of work and iteration, even with frontier models, in my experience.
However, building a framework, not even a shitty one, just an okay one, is not really hard. I know this because if you don't use a framework and you start building a website with an LLM, it will build a framework for you. The LLM might not have the feature breadth and definitely not the marketing dollars or ambition to sell you on its framework, but it still builds a framework. It'll make a framework just like it'll make functions, and classes, and all the typical abstractions we used to make when we programmed "by hand". Just because you're looking at it less doesn't mean the agent isn't fundamentally doing the exact same thing we're doing. I don't even care to call it slop, it's progressive feature adding with no cleanup, that's how I built all of my first projects. This is nothing new, the biggest thing that's changed is speed.
An agent can now build your website faster. It can look up information and ideas faster. It can create a mess faster. We were capable of all of these things before, this is not a "humans > AI at programming" take. My point is simply that you are either using an explicit framework, or generating an implicit one. If you don't think it matters at all, then to my earlier point, why even use React? You may not understand your bespoke framework, but your agent does and it wrote it and it probably likes it. You ask the LLM about its framework and it knows more about it than you know about React's internals, and it's just one step further along the inevitable pathway of merely having LLMs ship binaries instead of human-readable code. If that's what you believe, at least be honest about it and throw away React, surely it's only slowing you down.
If you do somehow, for some reason, think it's better that an LLM use a framework like React or a meta-framework like Next.js, my guess is it's because you prefer the LLM to use something battle-tested, well-abstracted, and well-documented. You probably also like that it sets up guardrails for the agent, it avoids reinventing the

title: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts
content:
Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts
By Bill Toulas
October 12, 2026 12:27 PM 1
Ledger has confirmed that some of its devices distributed through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with a hardware implant that drained users' cryptocurrency wallets.
The company has been investigating reports of users losing funds from wallets purchased through CryptoBilis, a major Malaysia-based hardware wallet retailer operating across Southeast Asia.
Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware.
Ledger wallets are physical devices designed to securely store the private keys that control cryptocurrency assets and authorize transactions.
On October 9, Ledger said it had launched an investigation into user reports of cryptocurrency losses and asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices.
The next day, the company confirmed hardware tampering on at least one device, though it’s still unclear exactly how or when the devices were tampered with.
"Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger is reaching out to impacted users as part of the ongoing investigation," Ledger said.
The crypto wallet maker also noted that it was working with authorities to identify the perpetrator and bring them to justice.
“[...]Ledger recommends users who purchased a Ledger device from this reseller to not initiate set up if they have not yet done so. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with a new seed),” warned Ledger.
Yesterday, Ledger provided another update, confirming that all user reports of unexpected fund drains were linked to devices sold through CryptoBilis and describing the affected volume as “limited.”
While the company did not disclose the type of devices compromised in this supply-chain attack, reports online talk about a spy implant in Ledger X devices that blends with the legitimate hardware.
Mark Karpelès, currently leading Karpeles Lab Inc. and CTO at Shells.com, showed a picture of the new implant in Ledger X, saying that it was "quite an evolution" from previous versions featuring manually soldered wires.
Hardware implant inside Ledger X device
source: Mark Karpelès
The former CEO of Mt. Gox said the implant was concealed behind the screen, but its antenna cable would have indicated that something was wrong.
According to Karpelès, the malicious hardware captured the device's display output and button presses to identify the seed phrase, then transmitted it to the attacker over an LTE connection using an eSIM.
"Ledger Nano X are used to store crypto. The spy implants are used to steal whatever crypto you store in those Ledger Nano X," Karpelès explained.
Although the CEO did not name CryptoBilis as the vendor of the compromised LedgerX, he said the device was not purchased via Ledger's recommended channels but from "a well known platform via a Chinese seller (product shipped from Malaysia)."
Tibane Labs, a cryptocurrency research and development studio, confirmed Karpelès' finding, adding that there were two implant versions for Ledger X.
The researchers obtained two variants, one in a Ledger device bought on Amazon Japan from " China-based seller · shipped from Malaysia," the other purchased on Yahoo! Auctions, Japan.
In a report over the weekend, Tibane Labs notes that the threat actor made room for the malicious circuitry by replacing the original battery with a smaller one, which powers both the implant and the Ledger X.
"Under the battery and antenna sits an ST STM32G431KBU6 (Arm Cortex‑M4, 128 KB flash, UFQFPN‑32)," the researchers found inside one of the devices.
For connectivity, the actor used "a tiny eSIM, an 8‑pad package just 2×2 mm, next to the MCU, and a shielded LTE module that sends the words out."
In the second hardware wallet analyzed, Tibane researchers found that markings on both the MCU (Microcontroller Unit) and the eSIM had been scraped off to hide the part numbers.
The second variant, which appears to be the same one that Karpelès described, is more advanced. It ran on the original battery and fit into the space normally occupied by the foam padding under the OLED display.
In both cases, the tell tale was the antenna wire, which ran along the top edge in the case of the second implant. In the first implant, the antenna is taped across the top of the battery and the shielded LTE module.
Hardware implant inside Ledger X
source: Tibane Labs
The researchers warned that the specimen above used "a designed, panelised flex PCB, the kind ordered from a board house, not a hand-built one-off."
Ledger is advising users to avoid purchasing from unauthorized resellers as they run an increased risk of getting counterfeit or modified devices.
The company is also reminding its authorized resellers and distributors to get the products only through authorized channels and to avoid restocking returned products.
Ledger provides a ‘Genuine Check’ mechanism to determine the authenticity of the device; however, it explicitly warns that it cannot detect added implants when the device’s original Secure Element remains intact.
At this time, there’s no indication that any other Ledger resellers are shipping compromised wallets; however, the community’s trust in the resellers’ network has been compromised, with many now calling for its dismantling.

Press Release
An Important Update About Grace Hopper Celebration
It is with deep regret that we are announcing the cancellation of this year’s Grace Hopper Celebration in Anaheim, CA.
This is not a decision we made lightly; we understand it leaves many of our community disappointed. It is a function of not having the funds required to move forward with the Celebration, unlike in years past. Unlike past events, this year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below our expectations and, ultimately, below the level needed to cover critical operating expenses.
We know this decision affects far more than an event. Many of you have made travel arrangements, booked hotels, received visas, secured time away from work, organized teams, and planned important moments around being together. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this creates.
If you have plans to attend GHC, please take the following steps now:
Cancel or modify your airline, train, or other travel reservations directly with your travel provider.
Cancel hotel reservations made independently directly with the hotel or booking provider, and any other reservations or commitments connected to your trip.
Information regarding GHC registration, sponsorships, exhibitor commitments, and other financial matters will be communicated directly to the individuals and organizations affected. AnitaB.org will contact registrants about registration fees by October 26. We recognize that each person’s circumstances may be different.
For questions or assistance specifically related to the cancellation, please contact [GHC@AnitaB.org]. We ask that you use this address so we can centralize inquiries and respond as effectively as possible.
To our attendees, sponsors, speakers, volunteers, partners, and everyone who has invested in making Grace Hopper Celebration possible: we are profoundly grateful, and profoundly sorry.
GHC has always been about more than a place or a moment on the calendar. It is about a community that has spent decades opening doors, expanding opportunity, and making sure women technologists have a voice in shaping the future of technology.
GHC has been central to our mission, and the circumstances leading to its cancellation have adversely affected our finances. We are evaluating strategic alternatives and the type of programming we can offer in the future. I anticipate further announcements will be made in the coming weeks as we gain greater clarity on key variables.
Brenda Darden Wilkerson
President & CEO
AnitaB.org

title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic \ Anthropic
content:
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.
In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.
Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026.
In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.
Growing our monorepo
Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.
Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.
As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.
Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.
The typical setup for scaling git checkouts.
Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?
Principles for agent-scale source control
With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling, so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:
Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.
Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.
A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.
Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.
Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.
The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.
How Scion works
It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.
Data structures
In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.
The shape of a changeset in Scion.
This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.
A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.
This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.
Scaling Scion
A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.
Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.
Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.
In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed.
The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system.
Scion’s checkout architecture.
Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs.
What we learned building Scion
We started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it.
Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures.
Merged changes to the Scion and Antique codebases per week, from January to September 2026.
What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like.
Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying

in Art | October 12th, 2026 Leave a Comment

There’s ahead of its time, then there’s Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau — or, in its orig­i­nal Dutch title, Klaer Ligh­t­ende Spiegel der Ver­fkon­st, a 900-page book of paint col­ors made before any such things were com­mon tools of the artist’s, scientist’s, and indus­tri­al designer’s trade. Author and artist A. Boogert cre­at­ed one, and only one, copy of his extra­or­di­nary man­u­al on col­or mix­ing in 1692. Appear­ing on the thresh­old of mod­ern col­or the­o­ry, and fea­tur­ing over 700 pages of col­or swatch­es, the book draws on Aristotle’s sys­tem of col­or rather than the new under­stand­ing of the col­or spec­trum, ful­ly elab­o­rat­ed by New­ton in his Opticks over a decade lat­er.
It would be anoth­er hun­dred years before a flood tide of col­or books began to make the the­o­ry more prac­ti­cal: from Goethe’s 1810 The­o­ry of Col­ors and Werner’s 1814 Nomen­cla­ture of Colour to the dream of col­or stan­dard­iza­tion real­ized: the Pan­tone com­pa­ny, launched in 1963.
But if A. Boogert had much influ­ence on the the­o­ry or prac­ti­cal appli­ca­tion of col­or in his day, there doesn’t seem to be much evi­dence for it. Of course most of the Dutch mas­ters had died when the book was com­plet­ed, and it seems unlike­ly that those still work­ing in 1692 would have been famil­iar with its sin­gle copy.
Instead, the book was meant to edu­cate water­col­orists, hence its French title, which refers to “water-based paint.” (A lit­er­al trans­la­tion of the Dutch runs some­thing like “clear­ly light­ing mir­ror of the paint­ing art.”) Medieval his­to­ri­an Erik Kwakkel found the book in a French data­base, “and it turns out to be quite spe­cial,” he writes, “because it pro­vides an unusu­al peek into the work­shop of 17th-cen­tu­ry painters and illus­tra­tors.
In over 700 pages of hand­writ­ten Dutch, the author, who iden­ti­fies him­self as A. Boogert, describes how to make water­colour paints. He explains how to mix the colours and how to change their tone by adding ‘one, two or three por­tions of water.’… In the 17th Cen­tu­ry, an age known as the Gold­en Age of Dutch Paint­ing, this man­u­al would have hit the right spot.”
The book is cur­rent­ly housed at Bib­lio­thèque Méjanes in Aix-en-Provence, where you’ll find full-page, zoomable, hi-res­o­lu­tion scans. “Beyond being infor­ma­tion­al, the images from the book are stun­ning and addic­tive flip through,” notes Refinery29. “They resem­ble page after page of Pan­tone col­or chips, except with­out the house­hold name.” One won­ders if “A. Boogert” would have become a house­hold name had his book been print­ed and dis­trib­uted. But his col­or sys­tem was already pass­ing away in the New­ton­ian age of col­or spec­trums and wheels, until paint chips final­ly came back in style. Vis­it the col­or man­u­al online here.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.
Relat­ed Con­tent: 
Goethe’s Col­or­ful & Abstract Illus­tra­tions for His 1810 Trea­tise, The­o­ry of Col­ors: Scans of the First Edi­tion
Werner’s Nomen­cla­ture of Colour, the 19th-Cen­tu­ry “Col­or Dic­tio­nary” Used by Charles Dar­win (1814)
The Vibrant Col­or Wheels Designed by Goethe, New­ton & Oth­er The­o­rists of Col­or (1665–1810)
Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

October 18, 2022
Sound
Invisible and relentless, sound is seemingly just there, traveling through our surroundings to carry beautiful music or annoying noises. In this article I’ll explain what sound is, how it’s created and propagated.
Throughout this presentation you will be hearing different sounds, which you will often play yourself on little keyboards like the one below. You can either click its keys with your mouse or use WER keys on your computer keyboard, but before you do so make sure your system volume is at a reasonable level:
W
220 Hz
E
330 Hz
R
440 Hz
We’ll eventually understand how these sounds are created and how they get to your ears, but we have to start by talking about the medium that is most commonly associated with sound – air.
Air
You’re probably aware that at microscopic level air consists of individual, tiny particles. Let’s look at the behavior of those molecules up close. In the demonstration below, I parceled out a tiny cube of air – notice how the molecules freely enter and leave this space. You can drag the cube around to change the viewing angle and you can also control the speed of the flow of time with the slider:
I need to note that this visualization simplifies things a little. The air consists primarily of nitrogen and oxygen – their particles contain two atoms bound together, but for simplicity I’m drawing all molecules as simple spheres.
Each particle of air travels through space with some velocity in a more or less random direction. While some molecules are faster, and some are slower, at room temperature the average velocity of a particle is a staggering 1510 ft/s so to make the particles visible I’m showing their motion significantly slowed down. As a side note, I’m using imperial units here, but you can switch to the metric system if you prefer.
With all the commotion in the previous simulation it may have been hard to see that the air particles collide with each other. In the demonstration below, I’m flashing the particles red and making them a little bigger right after they collide. To make these events easier to see you can control the speed of time with the slider:
Naturally, those particles can also collide with other things in the environment. In the simulation below I put up walls around that parcel of air. While at this scale we could also see the individual atoms constituting the walls of the box, I’m not showing them here to make things clearer. The particles of air are bouncing off these sides and every time that happens I’m drawing a little blue glow on the wall:
When an air particle bounces off, it imparts a small force on the wall. Although a single collision doesn’t do that much, with enough particles present the walls experience a constant barrage of collisions which exert expanding pressure on the container. The magnitude of that pressure is the sum of all these forces of impacts divided by the area of the box. Intuitively, for a box of a fixed size, the more particles there are, the heavier they are, and the faster they move, the higher the pressure.
Let’s see what happens if we resize this box a little while keeping the number of particles constant. In the demonstration below, you can drag the slider to change the length of the box, the plot in the bottom tracks the number of collisions per area of the box in a unit of time:
The number of collisions per area, and thus the pressure, increases as we squeeze particles closer together, and it decreases as we let them loose. Remember that we’re observing a significantly slowed down simulation. Because of the speeds involved here, I’m only letting you resize the box at a limited pace. That limitation prevents the walls from moving at enormous speeds, which would create some truly extreme pressure conditions.
It may not be immediately clear, but the experience of pressure is not limited to the walls of the box we built. Molecules in any open region of gas also experience compressing forces exerted by collisions with molecules from the neighboring regions. Those collisions aren’t as neatly aligned in space, but in aggregate it makes no difference if particles are bouncing off a wall or off particles from the neighboring area – the pressure is still there.
All the collisions between particles also have other consequences, but to look at them I need to adjust the scale at which we’ll be looking at – you can do this with a slider below:
The small cube of air from the previous demonstration is now just part of a larger volume. While this large cube is 20 times larger in each dimension, its sides measure only 1 micrometer – a few times smaller than a width of spider silk. Unfortunately, it would be both chaotic to display and taxing to correctly simulate the over 26 million air particles that one could find in this area. Instead, I’ll just visualize the motion of a single molecule as it travels through this space. In the demonstration below, I enlarged that particle to make it visible, you can also control the flow of time with the slider:
Due to collisions with other molecules, it may take a while for this particle to travel a significant distance and get out of this larger volume. You probably experienced this yourself – when someone sprays perfume in a distant part of a room the scent doesn’t instantly get to you. It’s only after some lucky aromatic particles manage to bounce into the vicinity of your nose that you get to experience the smell. If it wasn’t for the collisions with other molecules, those fragrant particles could travel the distance to your nose in a fraction of a second.
The important point is that, while the air particles move very fast, the collisions with other particles keep them mostly contained inside their local area. Over a longer period of time they will eventually all mix up, but at the short timeframes we’ll be interested in here, each reasonably sized parcel of air contains mostly the same particles.
All the microscopic behavior of individual particles we’ve observed ends up contributing to properties of air at larger scales. From this point on, we’ll move past looking at individual molecules and instead we’ll focus on regions of air that more closely match the sizes we’re used to. Those particles are still there, and they’re what actually end up distributing changes in gases, but we need to aggregate a huge collection of the molecules to end up with more discernible motions.
Let’s witness some of this large scale behavior when a section of air in a tube gets pushed on by a moving plate. In the demonstration below, I divided the air next to that circular plate into individual slices, which I’m drawing with thin lines. Although these boundaries are imaginary, they let us see what happens to different sections of air as you move the plate around with the slider:
Notice that the individual parcels of air move only a little from their initial position, but the disturbance caused by the motion of the plate seems to propagate through them with some speed. Moreover, that disturbance moves away from the plate regardless of the direction of the plate’s motion.
If you recall our experiment with a resized cube of air having more or less available space, you’ll notice that a very similar situation happens here inside each slice – this tells us that we’re witnessing some changes in pressure.
Let’s look at this situation from the side, which will make it easier to see how these pressure changes propagate. In the following demonstration I’m coloring each slice of air red when it’s compressed and the pressure increases, and I’m coloring it blue when it’s expanded and the pressure decreases:
When the plate moves to the right, it compresses the air particles in its vicinity, which increases the pressure in this region. Those particles then push and expand into particles in the neighboring slice of air, which then push onto the next slice and so on. All of this results in an area of higher pressure propagating away from the plate.
On the flip side, when the plate moves to the left, it creates an area of depletion, or rarefaction, which the neighboring slice of air rushes to fill in. This then reduces the pressure in the vicinity of the next slice and so on. While the slices move towards the receding plate, the pressure disturbance still moves away from the plate.
What we’ve just seen more clearly were pressure waves propagating through the air. When those pressure waves reach our ears we perceive them as sound. By moving the plate we’ve effectively created a very crude speaker that emits sounds as its moving element changes position.
While this simple demonstration helps to build an intuitive understanding of the propagation of pressure waves, the relation between the vibration of the object and the pressure disturbances it generates is much more complicated. We’ll soon explore some of those details, but for now we’ll focus on the relation between the movement of that vibrating element and the sound it produces.
Making Sounds
Let’s begin by introducing a simple musical instrument. By pressing a key down, you can request the plate to rapidly change its position. When you let that key go, the plate will move back by the same amount. Notice that each of the three keys moves the plate by a different amount, with red marker showing the total offset:
W
E
R
Despite its simplicity, this device lets us observe a few things. Firstly, a sudden jump of a plate creates a popping sound. It also doesn’t matter if the object has jumped forwards or backwards – the effect sounds the same.
Secondly, the loudness of that pop depends on the magnitude of the jump – the larger the jump the louder the pop.
Finally, this plate can jump forwards or backwards from any position – you can verify this by holding one of the keys and then pressing some other key. That pop sounds exactly the same as the sound created by a standalone key press.
Three pops of different loudness is not much to create music with as this only lets us play some simple beats. You may have tried pressing the buttons as fast as possible to create more upbeat tunes, but there are limits to how fast human fingers can press buttons.
Thankfully, we can ask the device you’re using to repeat the pops at a certain rate. In the demonstration below, you can drag the first slider to change how many times per second the plate should jump forwards and backwards. You can also control how far the plate moves with each jump using the second slider:
To describe the frequency of vibration, I’m using the unit of hertz, often abbreviated as Hz – it describes how many full cycles of motion happen within a single second. For example, a frequency of 2 Hz means that two full cycles happened in a second which means that the plate moved back and forth and back and forth again.
While at lower frequencies these patterns sound like a rapid series of pops, at higher frequencies these sounds blend together into a discernible note. The most important observation we can make here is that the higher the frequency with which the plate vibrates, the higher the perceived pitch of the resulting sound is.
You’ve probably observed that at lower rates you could follow the motion of the vibrating plate, but as the frequency increases, it becomes impossible to reliably track its movement. Unfortunately, we’re hitting the limits of frequencies we can easily display on a screen and perceive with our eyes, so from this point on I’ll significantly slow down the motion of the plate. The patterns of motion will still be correct, they’ll just happen at a much slower pace so that we can actually see what’s going on.
With that in mind, let’s make our music synthesizer create those very frequent jumps of the plate. We’ll assign a different frequency to each key – you can see them displayed above the keys. I’m also drawing three plots corresponding to each key, and an additional plot showing the cumulative effect of the individual motions.
These plots, or waveforms, represent the motion of the plate as requested by the keys. As the plots pass through the center line they reflect the current position of the plate, but remember that the motions we see here are a few hundred times slower than the actual ones:
W
E
R
Notice that when you press two keys at the same time you can still hear both sounds playing through – we’ve already seen that the final plate movement is just the sum of individual motions that each key requests.
You may also have realized that I’ve shifted the center line of the plate. What we consider a base position of that object is ultimately arbitrary. The keys simply request the plate to move forward or backward and they don’t care from where it’s starting, but having the object oscillate around a well defined origin will be more convenient.
If you look closely at the plots when two keys are pressed, you may have also noticed that there are some areas where one of the keys wants the plate to move forward, while the other wants it to move back. As a result, the plate stays at the same position.
What may be a little surprising is that there is nothing magical about the sound emitted by the plate when two keys are pressed – the emitted sound depends purely on the final movement of the plate. In the demonstration below, I made the third key emit the same pattern of motion as the combination of the first two:
W
E
R
The sound emitted when the third key is pressed is exactly the same as the sound emitted when the first two keys are pressed together. This is a very important observation, as it lets us explore some other patterns of motion that the keys could induce.
We’ll expand on this idea by changing the way in which the plate vibrates. Instead of having it rapidly jump back and forth, we can request the plate to move with constant velocity, following a triangular pattern. Let’s look at that pattern up close. Like other periodic shapes, a triangular waveform can be characterized by its amplitude, frequency, and phase:
In these visual examples the amplitude controls the height of the waveform. The frequency controls the width of the repeating pattern, which affects how many repetitions of the up-and-down triangles can fit inside a single second. The phase just shifts the shape around to change what we consider the beginning of that pattern.
We’ve already seen how the amplitude of the plate’s motion affects the perceived loudness, and this triangular motion is no different. In the demonstration below, all three keys move the plate in the same pattern, only their amplitude is different:
W
E
R
Similarly to the original rectangular pattern, we perceive different frequencies of this triangular motion as different pitches. In the following demonstration, each key has a different frequency as marked by the display in the upper part of the keyboard. The higher the frequency the higher the perceived pitch:
W
E
R

title: Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development - The Thunderbird Blog
content:
MOBILE
THUNDERBIRD
Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development
October 1, 2026
Aly Blenkin
30 responses
The team has been working hard behind the scenes laying a strong foundation for the Thunderbird iOS app. Rather than leveraging existing code, we are building natively from scratch. This fresh start allows us to take everything we’ve learned from Thunderbird Desktop and Android to ensure a fast, reliable, and modern experience on your iPhone right from the start.
Our ultimate goal is seamless cross-device experience. Whether you’re sitting at your desktop computer, checking messages on the go, your workflow should feel effortless and unified. 
Right now, we are focused heavily on getting the core foundations right. We are excited about the momentum because having clean architecture today means we can layer on exciting new features much faster in the future.
Below we’ve captured some of our work in progress. Nothing is final, but we wanted to share what we are cooking up so far. If you have feedback, keep reading on. At the bottom of the post we have  a link to a user research study where we want to hear from you and what you want to see from Thunderbird for iOS.
Hassle-free setup
Adding account user flow with options for email services like Google and Microsoft
We know people are really busy, often doing more than one thing at a time. We’re making login fast, secure, and fully automatic, so whether you’re signing in with a single click or setting up multiple accounts, you can get to your inbox quickly. 
Solid reliable connections
Thunderbird inbox
An email app is only as good as its connection. Behind the scenes, we’re building a background sync that maintains a steady connection with your provider that keeps your inbox up to date while respecting your battery life.
Core daily tools
Formatting toolbar (highlighted to show the details)
Your daily email routine should feel effortless. We’re polishing the essentials: a clutter-free, easy-to-read inbox layout paired with a clean, modern editor that lets you format messages smoothly without getting in your way.
Designed for growth
Thunderbird has always belonged to its community. We’re structuring the app with clean code and an experimental feature flag system so it’s easy for community developers to contribute. This means power users will be able to test out new experimental features early, and external contributors can easily help us extend what the app can do.
When can you try it?
Our goal is to have a first version ready for community testing in the next few months.
Building with our community, not just for people, is core to what we are trying to do. To help us decide what to build next after our first release, we’d love your input. If you had to pick the top three things that matter most to your daily email routine, what would they be?
➡️ Survey link
Update: the survey has now closed. Thanks to all that responded!
A note to the community 
Lastly, we know how long many of you have been asking for and waiting for Thunderbird on iOS. Whether you’ve dropped a comment on our forums, tagged us on social media, or simply kept an eye on our progress, thank you for your patience!
Bringing Thunderbird to iPhone and iPad isn’t just about building an app; it’s about doing it right so it serves you reliably for years to come. Today, we want to pop open the hood, share where we are, and work with everyone to design the best possible experience.

title: How random are you?
content:
Say numbers out loud, as randomly as you can, one after another. Don't think too hard, just keep them coming. Speak clearly, and if the house mishears one now and then, don't stop. The more numbers you say, the more accurate your result.
Before each one, the house seals its guess in an envelope. Say the number and the envelope opens.
You pick from 1 to 9. Your first 10 numbers are a warm-up while the house gets to know you. At the end, your ticket shows how you compare with 206 people from a psychology study.
DRAW NO. 0001
3
7
1
5
4
9
2
6
7
1
5
3
8
6
Pick your game
HOW YOU'LL PLAY
Say them
Type them
SPEECH PACK
The page listens to you inside your browser. The speech pack (about 31 MB) downloads once and stays on this device unless your browser clears it. Your audio never leaves the page.
Download the speech pack
Start the draw
How the house reads you
The house runs ten small predictors at once and trusts whichever has been right lately. Some count which number tends to follow which. Some track your steps up and down. One looks for the last time you said the same few numbers in a row, and one notices which numbers you haven't said for a while. That last one does most of the work, because people keep reaching for the numbers they've neglected. In a truly random sequence, each number is independent of the ones before it.
It gets a head start from 418 people who each picked 200 numbers from 1 to 9 in a psychology study, then adjusts to you as you go. Your first 10 numbers are a warm-up: the house guesses, but nothing counts yet. The more numbers you say, the more the house learns about you, and the more reliable your result.
