title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic \ Anthropic
content:
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.
In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.
Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026.
In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.
Growing our monorepo
Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.
Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.
As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.
Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.
The typical setup for scaling git checkouts.
Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?
Principles for agent-scale source control
With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling, so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:
Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.
Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.
A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.
Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.
Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.
The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.
How Scion works
It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.
Data structures
In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.
The shape of a changeset in Scion.
This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.
A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.
This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.
Scaling Scion
A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.
Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.
Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.
In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed.
The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system.
Scion’s checkout architecture.
Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs.
What we learned building Scion
We started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it.
Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures.
Merged changes to the Scion and Antique codebases per week, from January to September 2026.
What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like.
Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying

in Art | October 12th, 2026 Leave a Comment
Bluesky
Facebook

Email

There’s ahead of its time, then there’s Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau — or, in its orig­i­nal Dutch title, Klaer Ligh­t­ende Spiegel der Ver­fkon­st, a 900-page book of paint col­ors made before any such things were com­mon tools of the artist’s, scientist’s, and indus­tri­al designer’s trade. Author and artist A. Boogert cre­at­ed one, and only one, copy of his extra­or­di­nary man­u­al on col­or mix­ing in 1692. Appear­ing on the thresh­old of mod­ern col­or the­o­ry, and fea­tur­ing over 700 pages of col­or swatch­es, the book draws on Aristotle’s sys­tem of col­or rather than the new under­stand­ing of the col­or spec­trum, ful­ly elab­o­rat­ed by New­ton in his Opticks over a decade lat­er.
It would be anoth­er hun­dred years before a flood tide of col­or books began to make the the­o­ry more prac­ti­cal: from Goethe’s 1810 The­o­ry of Col­ors and Werner’s 1814 Nomen­cla­ture of Colour to the dream of col­or stan­dard­iza­tion real­ized: the Pan­tone com­pa­ny, launched in 1963.
But if A. Boogert had much influ­ence on the the­o­ry or prac­ti­cal appli­ca­tion of col­or in his day, there doesn’t seem to be much evi­dence for it. Of course most of the Dutch mas­ters had died when the book was com­plet­ed, and it seems unlike­ly that those still work­ing in 1692 would have been famil­iar with its sin­gle copy.
Instead, the book was meant to edu­cate water­col­orists, hence its French title, which refers to “water-based paint.” (A lit­er­al trans­la­tion of the Dutch runs some­thing like “clear­ly light­ing mir­ror of the paint­ing art.”) Medieval his­to­ri­an Erik Kwakkel found the book in a French data­base, “and it turns out to be quite spe­cial,” he writes, “because it pro­vides an unusu­al peek into the work­shop of 17th-cen­tu­ry painters and illus­tra­tors.
In over 700 pages of hand­writ­ten Dutch, the author, who iden­ti­fies him­self as A. Boogert, describes how to make water­colour paints. He explains how to mix the colours and how to change their tone by adding ‘one, two or three por­tions of water.’… In the 17th Cen­tu­ry, an age known as the Gold­en Age of Dutch Paint­ing, this man­u­al would have hit the right spot.”
The book is cur­rent­ly housed at Bib­lio­thèque Méjanes in Aix-en-Provence, where you’ll find full-page, zoomable, hi-res­o­lu­tion scans. “Beyond being infor­ma­tion­al, the images from the book are stun­ning and addic­tive flip through,” notes Refinery29. “They resem­ble page after page of Pan­tone col­or chips, except with­out the house­hold name.” One won­ders if “A. Boogert” would have become a house­hold name had his book been print­ed and dis­trib­uted. But his col­or sys­tem was already pass­ing away in the New­ton­ian age of col­or spec­trums and wheels, until paint chips final­ly came back in style. Vis­it the col­or man­u­al online here.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.
Relat­ed Con­tent: 
Goethe’s Col­or­ful & Abstract Illus­tra­tions for His 1810 Trea­tise, The­o­ry of Col­ors: Scans of the First Edi­tion
Werner’s Nomen­cla­ture of Colour, the 19th-Cen­tu­ry “Col­or Dic­tio­nary” Used by Charles Dar­win (1814)
The Vibrant Col­or Wheels Designed by Goethe, New­ton & Oth­er The­o­rists of Col­or (1665–1810)
Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

title: Press-Release
content:
Press Release
An Important Update About Grace Hopper Celebration
It is with deep regret that we are announcing the cancellation of this year’s Grace Hopper Celebration in Anaheim, CA.
This is not a decision we made lightly; we understand it leaves many of our community disappointed. It is a function of not having the funds required to move forward with the Celebration, unlike in years past. Unlike past events, this year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below our expectations and, ultimately, below the level needed to cover critical operating expenses.
We know this decision affects far more than an event. Many of you have made travel arrangements, booked hotels, received visas, secured time away from work, organized teams, and planned important moments around being together. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this creates.
If you have plans to attend GHC, please take the following steps now:
Cancel or modify your airline, train, or other travel reservations directly with your travel provider.
Cancel hotel reservations made independently directly with the hotel or booking provider, and any other reservations or commitments connected to your trip.
Information regarding GHC registration, sponsorships, exhibitor commitments, and other financial matters will be communicated directly to the individuals and organizations affected. AnitaB.org will contact registrants about registration fees by October 26. We recognize that each person’s circumstances may be different.
For questions or assistance specifically related to the cancellation, please contact [GHC@AnitaB.org]. We ask that you use this address so we can centralize inquiries and respond as effectively as possible.
To our attendees, sponsors, speakers, volunteers, partners, and everyone who has invested in making Grace Hopper Celebration possible: we are profoundly grateful, and profoundly sorry.
GHC has always been about more than a place or a moment on the calendar. It is about a community that has spent decades opening doors, expanding opportunity, and making sure women technologists have a voice in shaping the future of technology.
GHC has been central to our mission, and the circumstances leading to its cancellation have adversely affected our finances. We are evaluating strategic alternatives and the type of programming we can offer in the future. I anticipate further announcements will be made in the coming weeks as we gain greater clarity on key variables.
Brenda Darden Wilkerson
President & CEO
AnitaB.org

title: Anthropic conjures another threat that doesn't exist yet to stoke fears of AI apocalypse
content:
AI AND ML
Anthropic conjures another threat that doesn't exist yet to stoke fears of AI apocalypse
Self-replicating AI botnets could become feasible on IoT hardware within months, claims the Claude maker, if smaller models get smarter
Brandon Vigliarolo
GOVERNMENT AND IT NEWS REPORTER
11
Published Tue 13 Oct 2026 // 16:49 UTC
Make us preferred on Google
READ MORE
Ransomware gets personal: 'We-know-where-you-are kind of stuff'
now
Anthropic reinvents source control as Claude floods the world with code
6 hours ago
Claude submitted fake murder tip to Philly police during summertime testing
11 hours ago
Cheap Chinese and open source LLMs could trigger trillion-dollar AI infrastructure 'reset'
12 hours ago
Cyberattacks crank French supermarket refrigeration systems up to 50°C
17 hours ago
Nothing sells AI products as well as fear. Using new research, Anthropic claims that self-replicating AI worms could be just months away from spreading across vulnerable IoT devices, which would be a problem if it came true.
The frontier lab published a research report Monday suggesting that AI models could eventually self-replicate without relying on datacenter hardware, with a 9-billion-parameter model successfully setting up inference on eight of the nine hardware types Anthropic tested.
“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off,” Anthropic warned, adding that such an AI worm could also suss out the workings of unfamiliar devices, potentially making it more adaptable than conventional botnets like Mirai, Kimwolf (the representative IoT botnet threat model used in the study), and others.
Anthropic’s researchers managed to get a distributed instance of Gemma4-26B-A4B running across 15 generic Android set-top streaming boxes - a common target of traditional botnet malware due to their lax security. Once up and running, the distributed Gemma4 model was able to conduct inference tasks at a blistering 0.39 tokens per second. 
That, says Anthropic, proves that AI models can conduct inference with their various layers distributed across cheap hardware, but it doesn't prove such a model could self-replicate. For that, the researchers turned to Z.ai’s GLM 5.2. 
GLM was used to propagate a copy of Llama3.1-8B across eight Google Cloud instances running an Android 15 emulator in a virtual private cloud, which Anthropic said it was able to do with a high degree of success, with the model successfully spreading to all eight nodes in four out of five trials, and seven of eight in the other. 
“It appears that GLM-5.2 is able to propagate Llama3.1-8B well, which suggests that future small models of the same capability level could also complete the network enumeration, payload delivery, and inference standup steps of the replication process,” Anthropic explained. 
Sanity check: This isn’t going to end the world, either
Frontier AI labs have become adept at publishing findings that portend doom that only they can prevent. Doing more than a cursory reading of this report suggests that this threat is just as deserving of a big, honking asterisk as the rest.
Take, for example, what is needed for an AI model to exploit vulnerabilities and spread to various systems. One would think that such an element would be an important part of demonstrating the danger of a self-replicating AI botnet, but Anthropic decided it didn’t need to worry about that for this study. 
“We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process, since earlier papers CyberGym, ExploitBench, and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools,” Anthropic explained in the writeup.
In other words, the replication these models managed to achieve was done on nodes that were custom-built for this project and deliberately left open to attack, although the draggingly slow inference demonstration ran on real, inexpensive Android TV boxes. As Anthropic notes, AI models can also benefit from being given the right tools to turn them into capable cyberattack agents. There was a custom-built harness called Memento involved in this scenario too. 
Are IoT nodes that get hijacked by botnets famously insecure? Yes, but it doesn’t take much to prevent the most common ingress routes – that’s just good security hygiene that has nothing to do with the involvement of AI. Anthropic acknowledged that its deliberately simplified exploitation tests provided “an upper bound on real-world success.”
Then there’s the aforementioned speed. Anthropic says such AI worms would be challenging to shut down, but estimates that they might take days to double in size. When Mirai appeared on the scene in 2016, it was doubling in around an hour. 
Anthropic points out that speed is a factor in detection and mitigation, too. AI models are not simple malware packages: They’re massive things that would eat up tons of bandwidth and quickly point to their sources. As an AI botnet grew, that traffic could become more noticeable, making infected devices easier to detect.
Finally, end-to-end replication may have been successful with GLM-5.2, but that’s it. Anthropic tested other open-weight models, and they all “fail[ed] reliably,” according to the report. Anthropic didn’t mention how many models it tested. The report also mentions that GLM’s unique success has another important condition: It assumes its capabilities “could be packed into Llama3.1-8B,” stacking another assumption onto this latest house of doomsaying AI cards.
“Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end,” Anthropic said, while noting that GLM-5.2 was capable of end-to-end replication, conveniently leaving out all the important caveats. 
Anthropic further admits that it has no idea "exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take,” or when it might arise, if ever. “If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year,” the company added – again imposing an essential condition on this supposed threat. 
“As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control,” the company said at the end of its report. “We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.”
Here to stay for a given value of not existing yet, of course. Yet again, a frontier lab is warning us of a threat that doesn’t exist yet – at least in this case, basic security measures could make life harder for any future AI-powered botnet.  ®

title: Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development - The Thunderbird Blog
content:
MOBILE
THUNDERBIRD
Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development
October 1, 2026
Aly Blenkin
30 responses
The team has been working hard behind the scenes laying a strong foundation for the Thunderbird iOS app. Rather than leveraging existing code, we are building natively from scratch. This fresh start allows us to take everything we’ve learned from Thunderbird Desktop and Android to ensure a fast, reliable, and modern experience on your iPhone right from the start.
Our ultimate goal is seamless cross-device experience. Whether you’re sitting at your desktop computer, checking messages on the go, your workflow should feel effortless and unified. 
Right now, we are focused heavily on getting the core foundations right. We are excited about the momentum because having clean architecture today means we can layer on exciting new features much faster in the future.
Below we’ve captured some of our work in progress. Nothing is final, but we wanted to share what we are cooking up so far. If you have feedback, keep reading on. At the bottom of the post we have  a link to a user research study where we want to hear from you and what you want to see from Thunderbird for iOS.
Hassle-free setup
Adding account user flow with options for email services like Google and Microsoft
We know people are really busy, often doing more than one thing at a time. We’re making login fast, secure, and fully automatic, so whether you’re signing in with a single click or setting up multiple accounts, you can get to your inbox quickly. 
Solid reliable connections
Thunderbird inbox
An email app is only as good as its connection. Behind the scenes, we’re building a background sync that maintains a steady connection with your provider that keeps your inbox up to date while respecting your battery life.
Core daily tools
Formatting toolbar (highlighted to show the details)
Your daily email routine should feel effortless. We’re polishing the essentials: a clutter-free, easy-to-read inbox layout paired with a clean, modern editor that lets you format messages smoothly without getting in your way.
Designed for growth
Thunderbird has always belonged to its community. We’re structuring the app with clean code and an experimental feature flag system so it’s easy for community developers to contribute. This means power users will be able to test out new experimental features early, and external contributors can easily help us extend what the app can do.
When can you try it?
Our goal is to have a first version ready for community testing in the next few months.
Building with our community, not just for people, is core to what we are trying to do. To help us decide what to build next after our first release, we’d love your input. If you had to pick the top three things that matter most to your daily email routine, what would they be?
➡️ Survey link
Update: the survey has now closed. Thanks to all that responded!
A note to the community 
Lastly, we know how long many of you have been asking for and waiting for Thunderbird on iOS. Whether you’ve dropped a comment on our forums, tagged us on social media, or simply kept an eye on our progress, thank you for your patience!
Bringing Thunderbird to iPhone and iPad isn’t just about building an app; it’s about doing it right so it serves you reliably for years to come. Today, we want to pop open the hood, share where we are, and work with everyone to design the best possible experience.

Data InsightsElectricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak
OCTOBER 03, 2026
Electricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peak
Hannah Ritchie
Download
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.
Explore how electricity generation has changed in your own country
Related topic pages:
Energy

YESTERDAY
China reduced extreme poverty fast, but Indonesia hasn’t been far behind
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero.
Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong: many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart.
In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The
OCTOBER 10
What share of plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
Hannah Ritchie
Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:
A) Less than 1%
B) Less than 36%
OCTOBER 8
The new Living Planet Index reports a 73% average decline in studied wildlife populations
Hannah Ritchie
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
OCTOBER 6
Child mortality has declined in all world regions
Max Roser
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
OCTOBER 1
Europe is older, but Latin America is aging faster
Esteban Ortiz-Ospina
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
SEPTEMBER 29
The United States is the world’s largest oil producer
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
When people think about global oil, their minds often go toward countries in the Middle East.
But it’s the United States that is the world’s largest oil producer.
The chart shows oil production by country since 1990. As you can see, the US has been the largest producer for the last nine years, since it overtook Saudi Arabia.
Production in the US gradually declined during the 1990s and early 2000s, then increased sharply after 2010 and is now at an all-time high.
This data comes from the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy.

content:
Sammy's Blog
Table of Contents

11. Modern Monetary Theory and You
12. The Perfect Camera
13. Camera Lenses: What's in My Bag
14. Why Many Primary Forecasts are Wrong
15. The Wonky Math behind the Democratic Primary
16. What's Going on With The Impeachment
17. Treating Cancer with Chemo (Part 3)

20. The Importance of Doing Nothing
21. Why I Support Citizens United

rss
I posted to HN, and then my website was flooded with AI BOT traffic
For the past few years, I've been working on sprinklz.io, a customizable feed reader that can, among other things, deprioritize certain topics from your news feed.
A month ago, I posted it to HN, and it got a hundred or so upvotes, nice! It seems like people are really tired of hearing about LLMs, and they enjoyed being able to deprioritize them from their feed. It was a good demo of why a tool like this is useful. Everything was looking up, and then…
My website got slow. Like, really, painfully slow. At first I chalked it up to the extra attention of a suddenly popular post. Like any developer I both celebrated, and vowed to make my website more resiliant in the future. Strangely though, the slowness continued, and even started to get worse several days after my post went live, and the metrics I did log did not make sense. Like, you know, a good handful of genuinely active, logged-in users, and a sever exhibiting exhorbatantly high load.
So I took a look at some data. I added top-level logging for every endpoint (how many times was a request made to each url path), and I found that a majority of the requests did not even make an attempt to fetch news articles! For reference, my website is built as a single-page-application, and what this means is that a majority of the requests did not even run the javascript necessary to render the page (!).
Digging further, I looked at aggregate NGINX logs to find abusers, and, you're never going to believe this, but it turns out that nearly half of our traffic was coming from one specific user. I won't name names, but I looked them up, and they describe themselves as a service that listens for changes to a website, and then summarizes them into an AI slop news letter. And by 'listens to changes' I mean query our website many many times per-minute. Blocked.
Several of the others were your standard known crawlers, and kindly identified themselves as such. Claude bot, OpenAI bot, google's search indexer, and several others. I even picked up a few vulnerability scanners along the way. At least, somebody is trying to access -/wp-content/phpinfo.php (my website is not a wordpress site). I added robots.txt to discourage most of the AI scanners, but allow google-bot and other search-related traffic, and asked claude to query all the vulnerability paths and mimic the scanners to make sure I wasn't leaking anything. I also added reasonable rate limits, etc., etc.
The most important lesson though, is that it's time to make my website faster. I want to be the website that can day handle xxx QPS of real traffic, and it should scale better than it did, even under heavy load. Inspired by this encounter, I've made quite a few improvements to the underlying infrastructure over the past few weeks, and these should result in pretty substantial performance gains for all users.
P.S. if you'd like to check it out, the website is fully free, and available here
The TLDR is that it lets you define your own customizations, in addition to things like the points totals from hacker news. You can use it to filter out topics, like AI or LLMs, but the topics are completely arbitrary and you can program your own customizations.
Using LLMs to Make the Emacs Web Browser Great Again
When I tell people about the emacs web browser, their first reaction is 'Wait emacs has a web browser?!', followed by, 'yeah… I guess that's kind of a web browser'.
The emacs web browser is designed to render webpages in a terminal-based, textonly environment and, well, it goes about exactly the way you'd expect. It works well on HTML-only, small-content websites, but not so good for anything else.
The problem is that emacs is primarily a text-only editor, but the modern internet is very much not plain-text based. Simple HTML, designed in the simple style of the 1990s has a clear translation into plain text, but modern UI design, with it's visual styling, heavy javascript, and just, overall chaos, not so much.
The emacs web browser would be great, if only we could find a way to go back in time…
Ok, so the plan is simple. We take modern webpages, rewrite their source code into old-school simply-styled HTML, and then pipe it through to the emacs web browser. We just need to find a way to do this easily and at scale.
So um, you didn't forget about LLMs did you? It's nice to be using them in a way that will hopefully reduce the amount of spam content in the world.
Basically, the plan is we write a program that:
Opens a webpage in firefox
Loads the page and runs all the javascript
Asks an LLM to generate a re-usable program that transforms the current-page's contents into simplified text
Inject the generated javascript into the firefox browser
Grab the new page source and forward it to emacs web browser.
Yeah, and so, I've been using it, and it runs very well. Like realistically I can use this on many webpages where eww (emacs web wowser) did not run previously.
Below are some examples of before and after:
The docs for Clojure's mapcat
Figure 1: (before) Using eww-readable
Figure 2: (after) Using simpleweb-simplify-page
It takes a moment to generate the initial modifier program, but once it's generated, it runs pretty fast, and during day-to-day browsing, it mostly doesn't need any extra LLM calls. I have been using it myself and enjoying the experience.
The source code lives here: https://github.com/sstraust/simpleweb
and is open-source, and free to install, etc., etc.
If technology got better, why did everything get worse?
I think we all know the answer to this: bad incentives.
Technology makes systems more productive, but it does not, in fact, make you in particular more productive. The tools that enable computers to be more efficient also enable people to be more efficient at exploiting your time, attention, and wellbeing. I'm talking neural nets babyyy.
I first noticed the problem in 2018. Or rather, I noticed that I had a problem, and that problem was spendinng 3 hours a day watching starcraft 2 replays and wondering where the time went, and how I managed to stay up til 2am again.
What's interesting to me is that I didn't have any of these problems until the late 2010s. I had a computer with an internet connection since at least the mid 2000s, and a smartphone with twitter and reddit and the like not long after. It's possible that I've gotten less resiliant over the years, but I have a sneaking suspiscion that it's the computers who changed.
I can't quite put my finger on it, but I have this sensation that every time I interact with a system or website, I'm playing this kind of adversarial game, where I'm trying to just go about my day, and maybe read a little article about computers, and they're trying to figure out a way to keep me on their site for just a little bit longer.
I also have this feeling that as software engineering has moved from a discipline of hobbyists and enthusiasts to leaders who increasingly developed through finance or business-minded tracks, we've found ourselves with these major tools that we used to love become both extremely bland and extremely profitable.
So what can we do it make it stop?
touch grass. really when the world is like this, i think the best solution is to just leave. it's not easy, especially when the planning is often online, but if you can set it up, I promise that a day in the park playing chess with your friends is better than any amount of time you can spend on the internet.
take to the streets. i think that protesting is effective, and more people should do it. if you're willing to take action, it models to others that they can take action.
stop coming back to the same machines. I think we all have this gamblers fallacy in us, where if it didn't pay out the first time, but it pays out sometimes, we try the machine again, but it doesn't really work like that. if you're losing money the lesson is to stop putting coins in the machine.
editor's note: I've been working on a free customizable news reader as a way to take out some of my frustrations with the modern internet. if you don't use this one, I recommend following individual blogs and websites, because it's so much better to just get off these big platforms entirely.
editors note 2: i haven't yet posted this latest article to my rss xml, because i'm not ready to send notifications for it yet. will add in the coming weeks.
Deft version 0.2.0
Now that deft 0.2.0 is released, I figure it's a good time to talk about what I built, and why I built it.
The point of Clojure's everything-is-a-map toolkit is that getters and setters are a waste of time. Clojure was built, in large part, in response to the crappy 2008 Java workflow, where you had to write getters, setters, and builders, and you took on all this bloat that nobody enjoyed.
The problem is that if you want to represent your data using the built-in defprotocol and defrecord, and you want to define functions that depend on the presence of a certain field, then the only way to encode that information into the protocol is to add getter and setter metohds to it. icky.
You can also use a combination of protocol + malli schema to represent this, but then when you use it, you need to specify 'this function takes as input something that both implements this protocol and implements this Malli schema'. Also icky.
What we want is something we can use in the style of defprotocol and defrecord, but gives us all the getters and setters and map-like stuff by default. The key insight is that if a field exists in a record, we get all the other good stuff, so we just need to add support for protocols with required keys.
Deft v0.2.0 adds support for namespaced keys in type and protocol definitions. i.e., you can now do:
(defp Positioned :required-keys [::pos - ::Point])
and
(deft Circle [::location/position radius])

(>Circle ::location/position [1 2] :radius 12)
this is useful because you can now define methods that depend on those fields being present i.e.:
(defp Gremlin :extends [location/Positioned])

(defmethod game-object/get-hitbox ::Gremlin [self]
  (js/Matter.Bodies.rectangle
   (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/x])
   (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/y])
   15 15))
Check it out!
https://github.com/sstraust/deft
How much LLMs is too much LLMs?
I finished reading On the Edge last week, and it was bad. Not that I don't respect Nate Silver. I respect him a lot. So when his seminal text on gambling and risk taking was a rambling mess, I was suprised and disappointed. Nevertheless, a completionist at heart, I trudged on, to the very end, where I was greeted with this message:
"ChatGPT was a significant help in writing this book, serving as a creative muse when coming up with things like chapter subheadings, metaphors, and analogies, and for refining my understanding of technical topics that are likely to be well represented in its corpus."
Technically he wrote the book by hand, and technically he typed the letters onto his keyboard, but you know, did he really? Did he put his whole thought and mind and being into every word on the page? Maybe. I'm reminded of the absolute classic [Simple Made Easy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SxdOUGdseq4), a video where so much of the core lecture is built on defining precise language, and saying exactly what you mean. When you offload that work, you don't just skip word choices, you skip that thinking, and you miss out on that organization and mental clarity.
In reading Nate's book, there's a real and noticeable difference between the language that feels baked into the organizational fabric of Nate's mentality, and the bits that were added on as an afterthought. The later chapters especially felt like they lacked that sort of mental compactification that cohesifies everything under one vision. I'm sad because this could have been a phenominal work, and it's clear that a lot of effort was made, especially into interviews and data collection, and it feels like it's just lacking that one last missing piece of insight to bring it all the way home.
So how much LLMs is too much LLMs? Well, when it comes to human connection, I'd say the answer is near zero. I don't want to read your AI generated e-mails, and I certainly don't want to read your AI generated essays. I'd much rather read your prompt instead, because I care about what you, yes, you personally think about, and I want to understand what you wanted to communicate.
Don't get me wrong, I love LLMs for the right purpose. I'd love to use LLMs on doctor's notes to build models that predict whether the flu is spreading. But when it comes to writing, especially this kind of writing, it just feels so unnecessary, because when you write down your thoughts, I already have exactly what I wanted, and it just feels so silly to add an extra stop in between.
As a poker player and game theorist, I'm sure Nate would appreciate the phrase "If you couldn't be bothered to write it, then I can't be bothered to read it". And you know, despite a belief that art can live separately from the artist, deep down for me this claim rings true. Not that the same words produced by a person are inherently different than the same words from an LLM, but it throws off my little Bayesian estimator a little.
If the smartest person I know spent 10,000 hours writing, editing, polishing, and publishing a 500 page novel, it tells me not just that the smartest person I know had some thoughts on a topic, but it tells me that they decided to spend 10,000 hours of their precious time, and of their precious energy to communicate this idea to me. It feels good that the time it took me to read it is porportional (and usually less than) the time it took you to write it, because it shows me that you care about the time and energy of creating this exchange.
And it's not just fully AI generated slop that hits this barrier. When you incorporate LLMs into your writing, even a little bit, you miss out on the ability to process your thoughts and create human connecti

title: How random are you?
content:
Say numbers out loud, as randomly as you can, one after another. Don't think too hard, just keep them coming. Speak clearly, and if the house mishears one now and then, don't stop. The more numbers you say, the more accurate your result.
Before each one, the house seals its guess in an envelope. Say the number and the envelope opens.
You pick from 1 to 9. Your first 10 numbers are a warm-up while the house gets to know you. At the end, your ticket shows how you compare with 206 people from a psychology study.
DRAW NO. 0001
3
7
1
5
4
9
2
6
7
1
5
3
8
6
Pick your game
HOW YOU'LL PLAY
Say them
Type them
SPEECH PACK
The page listens to you inside your browser. The speech pack (about 31 MB) downloads once and stays on this device unless your browser clears it. Your audio never leaves the page.
Download the speech pack
Start the draw
How the house reads you
The house runs ten small predictors at once and trusts whichever has been right lately. Some count which number tends to follow which. Some track your steps up and down. One looks for the last time you said the same few numbers in a row, and one notices which numbers you haven't said for a while. That last one does most of the work, because people keep reaching for the numbers they've neglected. In a truly random sequence, each number is independent of the ones before it.
It gets a head start from 418 people who each picked 200 numbers from 1 to 9 in a psychology study, then adjusts to you as you go. Your first 10 numbers are a warm-up: the house guesses, but nothing counts yet. The more numbers you say, the more the house learns about you, and the more reliable your result.

title: The Universe of Discourse : Maybe a better way to track the release history of a Git repo
content:
The Universe of Discourse









Tue, 06 Oct 2026
Maybe a better way to track the release history of a Git repo
While I was still at ZipRecruiter, our Git monorepo was developing an annoying problem: it had too many refs.
Whenever there was a deployment of any of the applications in the repo, to staging or to production, the deployment tool would create a tag object with a name like this:
refs/release/stg.www.our-app-2019-09-06T114410.954-0700-treesha-179dab6fd11bee5195f0f8e31cea3edfb86ae23b
The tag contained the name of the target tier of the deployment (stg here, for “staging”), the app name and class of hosts on which it ran, www.our-app in this case, the date and time, and the hash of the tree that was deployed. This made a complete record of what was deployed, where, and when.
After we had been doing this for a while, there were thousands of these tag objects. Git is well-designed for handling thousands of commits, but not for handling thousands of refs. Perhaps this has changed, but at the time, Git would store refs in a file called packed-refs, which, for each ref, contained an entry with the ref's name and the ID of the object to which it referred.
(As with all things Git, the actual situation is somewhat more complicated. These additional ramifications don't affect the following discussion.)
Any operation that required resolving a ref name to its object had to search through the packed-refs file, which was taking an appreciable amount of time, far more than was desirable for an operation that everyone did many times a day. This affected not just local operations but operations on the Git server as well, and it was clear that it was only going to get slower as time went on. Also, the outputs of commands like git fetch and git branch were becoming increasingly cluttered with the names of tag objects whose only purpose was to record release history.
It seemed reasonable to me record the deployment history in the repository, but using thousands of tag objects clearly had serious drawbacks. In addition to the performance problems, the metadata itself was purely a convention in the tag name format, not legible to Git itself. There was a tree ID there, but nothing enforcing the rule that the tag should refer to a commit with that tree.
Also, the tag objects themselves seemed poorly-designed for the purpose. One good reason for storing history data in the respoitory is to render it immutable. But tags aren't immutable! They can be deleted and new ones can be inserted at any time, with any names desired.
And more important: consider the most natural sort of question that someone might want answered by the release history:
When did we last deploy the www.our-app app to production?
The only way to answer this question was to get the full list of all tags, filter it for prod.www.our-app, then sort by date and take the last item.
Or similarly: What if the most recent staging deployment had turned out to be bad, and we wanted to immediately revert to the version before that? Again, we (or the reversion process) would have had to filter and sort a list of thousands of tags, then pick out the second-last one.
I proposed this alternative in 2019. It stores the deployment history of each app as a series of unnamed but related Git objects, using Git's own history mechanism, so it's simple, efficient, and meshes well with Git's commands.
I don't think it was ever adopted, and it might turn out to have serious drawbacks I haven't foreseen. But it might be useful to someone in a similar situation.
Maintaining an audit and reversion trail without thousands of refs
Currently, each time a new version of an app is deployed, we create a ref:
refs/release/stg.www.our-app-2019-09-06T114410.954-0700-treesha-179dab6fd11bee5195f0f8e31cea3edfb86ae23b
As these refs proliferate, many operations in the Git repo become slower and slower.
We can record this information in a way that is at least as useful and which doesn't clutter up the ref list.
Current practice
At present, the release procedure creates a ref something like this:
A new release is created at commit H
A new tag object is created, pointing to H, something like
git tag -a refs/release/stg.www.our-app-2019-09-.... H
Every new tag object has a name in the ref database. This adds a name for every release. The structure is something like this:
One ref object per release, each pointing to its own head commit
Alternative proposal
Each (tier, app) pair is represented by a linked list of release commits
The head of the list is the most recent release
One ref points to the head of the list
Older releases can be found by following the links back in time
Main point of this proposal: There is only one ref for each (tier, app) pair, no matter how many releases have been done.
It will look like this:
A chain of metainfo commits, each with the previous metainfo commit as first parent and the actual release commit as second parent
The one ref (which might or might not be an actual ref object) is named stg.www.our-app. That points not to the actual release commit, but to a commit that contains metainformation, such as the treesha. The metainformation could be stored in any of several ways. (See below.) The exact time of the release doesn't need to be stored explicitly because it is exactly the time at which the metainfo commit was created.
The metainfo commit has two parent commits. One is the actual release commit, the one that, in the current system, is the target of the named ref object. The other parent is the metainfo commit from the previous release.
The metainfo commits are chained together exactly the same way Git normally chains commit history, so the usual Git commands will work on the release history in reasonable and useful ways. In particular, the command git log stg.www.our-app will produce a listing of the release history.
Technical details
Creating this sort of two-parent commit is easy. Suppose the ref stg.www.our-app points to the current metainfo commit. And suppose we want to release new commit H. We do:
(Write some useful commit message into /tmp/message.$$.)
git commit-tree -p refs/release/stg.www.our-app -p H \
    H^{tree} < /tmp/message.$$
This creates a new metainfo commit with two parents, given by the arguments of the -p options. The first parent is the metainfo commit for the current release and the second is new commit H.
The git commit-tree command creates the new metainfo commit and writes its SHA on standard output. Say this SHA is N.
git push origin N:refs/release/stg.www.our-app
The release ref now points to the metainfo commit for the new release.
Usage
This will be easier to use than what we have now, because Git's command set was designed to manage a list of commits linked in this way; this is exactly how Git normally expects to represent history. This natural fit with Git's command set shows up in many places.
You can fetch a complete release history for any project with a single fetch:
git fetch origin refs/release/stg.www.our-app:HISTORY
After this, git log HISTORY will list the entire release history in reverse chronological order. All the usual git-log options make sense to filter or search this list. For example, if we want to find the last release before a certain date, we can use:
git log -1 --until=date HISTORY
If we want a forward-chronological list of release commit SHAs with their release dates, we could use something like:
    git log --reverse --format="%P %cd" HISTORY
At all times:
The current release commit is accessible at HISTORY^2.
The metainfo commit from n releases ago is at HISTORY~n.
The release commit from n releases ago is at HISTORY~n^2.
Notice: if M is a metainfo commit that describes a release, M^ is the metainfo commit for the release before that, and M^{2} is the exact commit that was actually released. We don't have to record the tree IDs in the ref names; the tree that was released in release M is M^{2}^{tree}. These notations will work as expected in all git commands; see git-rev-parse.
Because Git naturally understands this way of organizing history, it will be easy to locate a particular previous release for rollback. When we roll back, we can roll back to the exact same commit as before: the new metainfo commit and the old one can share the exact same release commit object.
We can see the differences between the last two releases, without knowing their exact dates, with something like:
    git diff HISTORY~1^2 HISTORY^2
The metainfo commit is a full commit with a full set of Git commit metadata, such as a creation date. It has a commit message where we can record any unstructured text that we want. We could also require the commit message to be in TOML format, or we could use the tooling provided by Git to store semi-structured information in the commit message; see git-interpret-trailers.
If the built-in commit structure is not big enough for everything we want to record, the metainfo commit also has an associated tree where we could record any amount of structured information. In the example above I had its tree be identical to the release commit's tree, which might be convenient. (That way, if you wanted to see the files that were released, you could look in either the release commit or the metainfo commit; this would make some of the commands simpler.) But the tree doesn't have to be the same. We could also add metainformation files to this tree, or we could commit an entirely unrelated tree with nothing in it other than structured metainformation.
Performance?
Ploni Almoni asks about the performance issues of tracing out a linked list of commits. But this is exactly the same mechanism that Git normally uses to record history. When we do git log, Git is tracing a linked list of commits in exactly the way suggested here. If any operation in Git is going to be fast, it will be this one.
Git currently takes a few seconds to trace the 275,000-commit history of our monorepo. Tracing the similarly-structured history of a few hundred release commits is not going to be an issue.
I wrote this originally, but my only copy was in the form of a PDF. I had Claude convert the PDF to Markdown, which is the native format accepted by my blog, and the two diagrams to SVG. I then substantially edited the text and the diagrams. Along the way Claude pointed out three minor errors, which I corrected. I also took Claude's advice on how to adjust the colors from the original to make them more legible to color-blind readers.
Every word was written by my brain using my fingers.

title: kcgi | minimal CGI and FastCGI library for C/C++
content:
BSD.lv tools for BCHS: kcgi, sqlbox, ort
kcgi – minimal CGI and FastCGI library for C/C++
Version 1.0.1
kcgi is an open source CGI and FastCGI library for C/C++ web applications. It is minimal, secure, and auditable. To start, install the library. Then read the deployment and usage guides.
Show source comments
The following echoes Hello, World! as an HTTP response to a CGI request.
#include <sys/types.h> /* size_t, ssize_t */
#include <stdarg.h> /* va_list */
#include <stddef.h> /* NULL */
#include <stdint.h> /* int64_t */
#include <kcgi.h>

int main(void) {
    struct kreq r;
    const char *page = "index";
    if (khttp_parse(&r, NULL, 0, &page, 1, 0) != KCGI_OK)
        return 1;
    khttp_head(&r, kresps[KRESP_STATUS], 
        "%s", khttps[KHTTP_200]);
    khttp_head(&r, kresps[KRESP_CONTENT_TYPE], 
        "%s", kmimetypes[KMIME_TEXT_PLAIN]);
    khttp_body(&r);
    khttp_puts(&r, "Hello, world!");
    khttp_free(&r);
    return 0;
}
For fuller examples, see sample.c (C and CGI), samplepp.cc (C++ and CGI), sample-fcgi.c (C and FastCGI), or jump to the Documentation section.
kcgi supports many features: auto-compression, handling of all HTTP input operations (query strings, cookies, page bodies, multipart) with validation, authentication, configurable output caching, request debugging, formatted writers (JSON, XML, etc.) and so on. Its strongest differentiating feature is using sandboxing and process separation for handling the untrusted input path.
current release
Version 1.0.1: 2025-11-17
Hot-fix 1.0.0 with proper naming of Mac OS X shared libraries, which use a different convention of version suffix than other Unix-like systems.
(release archive)
installation
First, check if kcgi isn't already packaged for your system, such as with pkg_add kcgi (OpenBSD), pkg install kcgi (FreeBSD), brew install kcgi (brew), pacman -S kcgi (Arch Linux), and so on. If so, install using that system.
If not, kcgi has been built and run on GNU/Linux (musl and glibc), OpenBSD, NetBSD, FreeBSD), Solaris, OmniOS, and Mac OS X (only Mojave and newer!) on i386, amd64, powerpc, arm64, and sparc64. Download kcgi.tgz and verify the archive with kcgi.tgz.sha512. To run bleeding-edge code between releases, the repository is on GitHub. In both cases, build and install instructions may be found on the repository page.
The only hard build-time dependency is BSD make (bmake on Linux) and zlib. If you're running the regression tests (see Testing), you'll also need libcurl.
deployment
To use kcgi, you'll need a web server capable of running CGI or FastCGI. Apache, nginx, and OpenBSD's httpd(8) have all been used extensively, with the latter two natively over FastCGI and via the slowcgi wrapper.
To compile kcgi applications, use the package configuration. Linking is similarly normative.
% cc `pkg-config --cflags kcgi` -c yourprog.c
% cc yourprog.o `pkg-config --libs kcgi`
Well-deployed web servers, such as the default OpenBSD server, by default are deployed within a chroot(2). If this is the case, you'll need to statically link your binary (or pull all shared libraries into the shadow root).
% cc -static yourprog.o `pkg-config --static --libs kcgi`
FastCGI applications may either be started directly by the web server (which is popular with Apache) or externally given a socket and kfcgi(8) (this method is normative for OpenBSD's httpd(8) and suggested for the security precautions taken by the wrapper).
documentation
The kcgi manpages, starting with kcgi(3), are the canonical source of documentation. The following is a list of all manpages:
