title: MIT class project turns into an FDA-cleared treatment for tremors | MIT News | Massachusetts Institute of Technology
content:
Wristband device from Encora Therapeutics started as a project in 2.009, MIT’s iconic product-design class.
Zach Winn | MIT News
Publication Date
October 2, 2026
PRESS INQUIRIES
Encora Therapeutics started as a class project in 2.009, in MIT’s iconic product-design class. The wearable is now an FDA-cleared treatment for tremors.
Credit: Courtesy of Encora Therapeutics
Previous image
Next image
In 2017, a man named Michael walked onto stage in front of a packed Kresge Auditorium at MIT and attempted to draw a spiral, a common test doctors use to diagnose Parkinson’s disease. His tremors, caused by the disease, made the exercise difficult. 
Then, Michael put on a wristband device made by a team of MIT students as part of 2.009 (Product Engineering Processes), who were presenting their prototype that evening.
Michael pressed a button and the device produced a subtle vibration. The vibration sent signals up his wrist and into his brain. His tremors dramatically decreased, and within seconds he was able to draw the spiral with much more precision, to a roaring ovation from the audience.
“When this device is turned on, I feel like I used to feel when I didn’t have Parkinson’s disease,” Michael told the crowd. “It’s an amazing, amazing feeling.”
The performance was so impressive that the student team received requests from classmates and others asking where they could buy the device for family and friends living with tremors. Unfortunately, the students had to explain there was only one — for the time being.
The event set off a near decade-long journey that began by leveraging MIT entrepreneurial resources like MIT Sandbox, MIT FUSE, and the MIT Venture Mentoring Service. In 2020, the student team turned into an official company, Encora Therapeutics. But there were still dozens of hardware iterations ahead. Then there were clinical trials. In one trial, 78 percent of patients reported benefits after 90 days of home use.
This February, nine years after Michael’s brave demonstration, all that work finally paid off: The FDA cleared Encora’s device to help adults with essential tremor, a condition similar to Parkinson’s that causes shaking, often in the hands. 
“It’s been a long and difficult — very difficult — journey, but also very rewarding, especially when we get feedback from patients,” says Daniel Carballo ’18, SM ’20, an Encora co-founder and vice president of strategy. “We hear stories from patients about how they’ve struggled with their condition and how much they benefit from this. It reminds us why we keep going.”
From classroom to commercialization
The three founders of Encora who are still with the company are Carballo, Allison Davanzo ’18, and Kyle Pina ’18. They were each seniors in 2017 when they enrolled in 2.009, MIT’s popular product-design class.
The semester began with a brainstorming session in which groups of about 17 students were asked to come up with dozens of potential product ideas. Carballo proposed a wearable device that used mechanical vibration to send signals to the brain to reduce tremors. The initial idea was to help patients with Parkinson’s disease.
“It was one of hundreds of throwaway ideas,” Carballo recalls. “The initial concept was inspired by classes I had taken in robotics around neural control of movement. I had a preliminary understanding of how an electromechanical device might interact with the body’s control systems and feedback loops that control movement to relieve pathological control of movement.”
The team eventually whittled their long list of ideas down to a few. Carballo’s idea was finally selected by a vote of 16-1 — with Carballo the only dissenting vote.
“I tried to explain to the team that this was so far-fetched that there was no way, in one semester, we would be able to make anything,” Carballo recalls. “Thankfully, I got outvoted.”
Through most of the semester, Carballo’s pessimism looked justified. At every class milestone, the team lagged behind other teams. Then, the week before final presentations, they met Michael, whose severe hand tremors were the result of early-onset Parkinson’s.
“He was a home renovator, so he worked with his hands, but his tremors had progressed to the point that he struggled to turn a screwdriver, use a drill, or even fill out paperwork,” Carballo recalls. “He had become reliant on his wife and daughter not only to run his business, but to help him with everyday activities.”
By this point, the 2.009 team had a prototype that would vibrate to send mechanical feedback to the brain. Carballo described it as “a foamcore box with a Raspberry Pi chip and some wires coming out.” When Michael put on the device and turned it on, his tremors dramatically decreased.
“It was like a light switch turned on and his tremors stopped,” Carballo says. “His wife and daughter started crying. A week later, he was gracious enough to repeat the process on stage for the final presentations.”
The presentation — and the outpouring of interest from people who wanted it for loved ones with Parkinson’s — made the team determined.
“It showed us there were a lot of people with this problem that could really benefit from this,” Carballo says. “A subset of the team became possessed. It would have been such a shame to know this could exist and to have it never leave the classroom.”
Some team members began using MIT’s entrepreneurial resources to commercialize the technology, initially focusing on Parkinson’s. They ran their first clinical trial with 20 Parkinson’s patients in 2022 in collaboration with MassGeneral Brigham. But they soon learned more patients are living with essential tremor.
“It was a greater unmet need,” Carballo says. “There are a lot of drugs being developed for Parkinson’s disease, but essential tremor hasn’t experienced that same innovation.”
Today scientists think tremor is caused by malfunctioning signals in the regions of the brain responsible for interpreting sensory input and coordinating movement.
“In these diseases, neurotransmitter deficiencies result in this pulsed signaling in the brain that manifests as tremors that are basically pulsed motor outputs,” Carballo says.
One current approach to target those signals is surgery that involves drilling holes in the skull to insert electrodes that drive new electrical patterns in the brain. Encora’s watch-like product targets the same brain regions with mechanical vibrations at the wrist.
“We’re applying mechanical stimulus, basically vibration, to stretch receptors in the wrist, which tell your body where it is in space,” Carballo explains. “The stimulation causes the receptors to activate and send a patterned signal to peripheral nerves of the wrist, that then carry the signal to the peripheral nervous system and into the central nervous system, to the same regions of the brain targeted by surgery.”
In 2024, Encora ran a randomized control trial with 47 patients living with essential tremor. Last year, the team ran a 59-person trial where patients used the devices at home. In both trials, more than 70 percent of patients experienced meaningful improvement.
The results were promising enough to gain what’s known as 510(k) clearance from the FDA for use as a medical device, in February of this year.
Helping patients
Most patients see rapid benefit when using Encora’s device. Patients have described the device as life-changing. Some say it allows them to do tasks they haven’t been able to do in years.
“We see some patients using the device 12, 14 hours a day,” Carballo says.
Today, Encora is focused on building a national sales force and working to secure coverage from insurers. As the company ramps up production, the product will finally become available for patients who qualify.
Further down the line, Encora hopes to fulfill its original mission of helping mitigate tremors in patients with Parkinson’s. Carballo believes the approach also holds promise for many other patients.
“There is a surprisingly long list of diseases that this could work for,” Carballo says.  “The most obvious are neurological movement disorders, but the bigger picture of wearable neuromodulation is a rapidly growing field that has seen therapeutic benefit across a broad range of diseases. We see this as a platform technology.”

title: AlphaNIST
content:
AlphaNIST
From AlphaGo to AlphaZero, reinforcement learning produced strategies that surprised expert players. AlphaZero learned from experience at scale, without human demonstrations.
AlphaNIST brings this philosophy to contact-rich, high-precision robotic assembly in simulation. An end-to-end policy learns how to complete the task, without prescribed manipulation stages.

The assembly challenge
NIST Assembly Task Board #1, shown fully assembled.
The NIST board has twenty assembly tasks, with parts as small as 4 mm. Fitting one part can take several changes of grasp and orientation. Tight clearances leave little room for error: a tilted nut can jam or cross-thread.
With several parts, the robot also has to choose an order. An installed component may block the gripper’s next move.
Robots can be creative—if we give them room.
Trying to prescribe every maneuver means anticipating how the robot should respond as contacts and obstructions change. A two-finger gripper may also need solutions quite different from those that come naturally to a human hand.
Perhaps the answer is to stop telling the robot how we think the task should be done, and let it learn how to get there. We give it a binary task reward for success and train it through vast amounts of diverse experience. That leaves room for the robot to discover solutions we might never have thought to teach.
How the robot learns
Experience diversity:
heterogeneous assets and initial states
One policy trains across twenty heterogeneous assemblies, starting from loose parts, in-hand grasps, and partial assemblies cached in simulation.
Near-complete starts let the robot practice finishing an assembly before it can solve the whole task. The cache supplies starting states, not demonstrations.

OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
Federal prosecutors say an employee from Saudi Arabia planted an audio recorder and left another unattended in his bag.
An OpenAI engineer concealed a recording device in a conference room used by executives at the company, the Department of Justice claims. |

By George Kelly and Michael McLaughlin

An OpenAI engineer has been arrested on suspicion of hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday and remains in custody.
An unattended bag found in the company’s offices contained Alfozan’s wallet and identification, as well as a recording device, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in San Francisco.

Alfozan has worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors said.
OpenAI personnel found the device Sept. 30. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and had been concealed in toilet paper, the complaint says. The company determined it was installed around Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted.

title: PostEra - Machine Learning Researcher - Agentic Science
content:
Machine Learning Researcher - Agentic Science
RemoteMachine Learning /Full-Time /Remote
APPLY FOR THIS JOB
PostEra is building an AI-first biotech. We use Proton, our AI platform for medicinal chemistry, to accelerate the discovery of new medicines for patients. PostEra is advancing an internal pipeline focused on Women's Health and Fertility, and has used Proton to nominate multiple clinical candidates across PMOS and Fertility. PostEra also advances small molecule programs through partnerships with pharma. We've closed over $1B in AI partnerships including 4 multi-year agreements with Pfizer and Amgen. PostEra is also leading an antiviral drug discovery center for pandemic preparedness, funded by one of the largest grants in NIH history. 
PostEra's Organizational Structure
We believe time spent navigating complex hierarchies in organizations is better invested in the pursuit of novel technology and scientific discoveries. As such, our organizational structure is intentionally minimalist. 
We promote a culture where individual achievement is celebrated through proportional compensation and internal recognition, including meaningful promotions.
Ultimately, our collective focus is delivering cures to patients, which we believe needs a huge amount of cross-disciplinary collaboration, so we've fitted our organizational structure to serve that end.

Role Overview
In this role, you will develop the agentic research vertical at PostEra, using agentic systems to automate the development of mechanistic models for biochemical and physiological processes, and analyse biological data for target validation. You will interact closely with chemists and biologists to use these models to drive drug discovery decisions. 
You will also develop machine learning methods that can rapidly adapt to new drug discovery problems from limited labeled data. A particular focus is molecular and tabular in-context learning and building foundation models from PostEra’s proprietary multimodal data. You will build models that use the context of drug discovery effectively, determine which prior examples and tasks are relevant, quantify when transfer is helpful or harmful, and provide reliable predictions under distribution shift. 
You will help drive the full research loop: defining tasks, constructing datasets and evaluation episodes, developing strong baselines, training and scaling models, performing rigorous ablations, and translating successful methods into capabilities used by PostEra’s scientists. Prior drug discovery experience is not required, but you should be motivated to learn the domain and work closely with medicinal chemists, computational chemists, and other scientists.
Key Responsibilities
Agentic Research for Chemistry and Biology: Develop and benchmark agentic systems to automate the development of quantitative models to simulate biological and physiological processes, and the analysis of biological data. 
Research Direction and Execution: Independently identify, formulate, and lead research projects involving in-context learning, agentic systems, few-shot adaptation, tabular foundation models, and molecular machine learning.
In-Context Learning for Molecules: Design and train models that adapt to new assays, endpoints, targets, or chemical series using limited labeled context and heterogeneous historical data.
Benchmarking: Rigorously compare new approaches against strong baselines, curating test cases that deconfounds impact of different sources of bias. 
Cross-Functional Collaboration: Work with scientists to connect modeling objectives and evaluation metrics to practical decisions in potency modeling, ADME prediction, selectivity, lead optimization, and the design of early clinical studies.
Model Training and Scaling: Develop efficient training and data pipelines and, where appropriate, scale models across large collections of molecular and tabular tasks.
Research Engineering: Produce readable, reproducible research code; maintain well-tracked experiments; and contribute through code review, documentation, and shared modeling infrastructure.
Scientific Dissemination: Publish results in leading machine learning, medicinal chemistry, or computational biology venues. You will be an ambassador of PostEra to the scientific community. 
Key Requirements
PhD degree in machine learning, or STEM research involving the development of novel machine learning approaches 
Track record of high-quality research, such as publications and open-source contributions
Strong research or engineering experience in modern machine learning, deep learning, or statistical modeling, backed by understanding of the theory behind machine learning algorithms
Demonstrated expertise in at least one relevant area: agentic workflows for science, machine learning approaches to bioinformatics and clinical data modelling, in-context learning, tabular learning, few-shot learning
Hands-on experience training, debugging, and evaluating ML models in Python using frameworks such as PyTorch or JAX
Ability to independently translate ambiguous scientific or technical problems into well-defined ML projects, including datasets, task definitions, baselines, metrics, and validation schemes
Ability to design careful experiments, benchmarks, and ablations that distinguish improvements from biases, and understand which aspects of the model led to the improvements
Comfort working in a startup environment where priorities evolve, data is imperfect, and high-quality judgment matters as much as raw model complexity
Nice to Haves
Candidates are more likely to succeed in this role if they also have experience with one or more of the following:
Training tabular foundation models, particularly for sparse, heterogeneous, small-data, or high-missingness settings
Developing molecular in-context learning systems or adapting general-purpose in-context models to molecular or scientific data
Large model training, including 1B+ parameter models, distributed training, sharding, data parallelism, model parallelism, and large-scale data pipelines
The development of AI “co-scientist” systems for physical or biological problems 
Hands-on experience in modelling biological, biochemical or clinical data using machine learning approaches 
Moving research models into production scientific software or computational workflows
Salary: 200k - 300k
Equity: 0.05 - 0.1%
Visa Sponsorship: Not at this time
Hiring Manager:  Alpha Lee

Visit us at postera.ai
We use recruiting software to support the hiring process, such as collecting, organizing, and managing applications. Applications are reviewed by our recruiting team, and we do not use artificial intelligence or automated decision-making tools to evaluate candidates or make hiring decisions. Human judgment is used throughout the hiring process, and all final decisions are made by our hiring team. If you would like more information about how your personal data is processed, or about your rights under applicable data protection laws, please contact us.

Note
Given that this issue has been shared online and is currently getting quite a few visitors, here's some additional context.
Rust's type system is intended to prevent memory unsafety. Upholding this promise is something we take very seriously, which is why we've been working on things like the next-generation trait solver, the region constraint rework, and more generally Project Zero. It is a large priority of the Types Team to fix all type system unsoundnesses and to work towards there being a solid foundation to minimize the risk of unknown ones.
This bug is a P-high issue and would have been P-critical regardless of whether people encountered it in the wild. The reason that it is "only P-high" is that it's 11 years old. A bug like this which has not been found during the last 11 years cannot actually be that easy to hit.
Looking at the bug itself, it is also very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident. While it looks easy to trigger, to exploit this you need an intentionally malicious Drop implementation.
~ @lcnr
In the following code:
use std::sync::Mutex;
static KEPT: Mutex<Vec<Box<dyn std::any::Any + Send>>> = Mutex::new(Vec::new());
struct Q<T: 'static + Send>(Option<T>);
impl<T: 'static + Send> Drop for Q<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) { if let Some(t) = self.0.take() { KEPT.lock().unwrap().push(Box::new(t)); } }
}
fn main() {
    {
        let l = String::from("hello world, this is long enough");
        let mut q = Q(None);
        q.0 = Some(&l);
    }
    let _z = String::from("XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX");
    let k = KEPT.lock().unwrap();
    println!("{}", k[0].downcast_ref::<&'static String>().unwrap());
}
I expected to see this happen: program is not accepted
Instead, this happened: program compiles and prints XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. With asan, the program will crash with a AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-scope
Meta

        ];

title: AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. - yyhh.org
content:
AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill.
Mon 12 October 2026 Huahai AI LLM Tools Clojure
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.
Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs.
One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful: it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its answers matter.
An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.
Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?
The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful.
Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does.
What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.
I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment.
The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

Thunderbird for iOS: A First Look at the Native iPhone Email App in Development
October 1, 2026
Aly Blenkin
30 responses
The team has been working hard behind the scenes laying a strong foundation for the Thunderbird iOS app. Rather than leveraging existing code, we are building natively from scratch. This fresh start allows us to take everything we’ve learned from Thunderbird Desktop and Android to ensure a fast, reliable, and modern experience on your iPhone right from the start.
Our ultimate goal is seamless cross-device experience. Whether you’re sitting at your desktop computer, checking messages on the go, your workflow should feel effortless and unified. 
Right now, we are focused heavily on getting the core foundations right. We are excited about the momentum because having clean architecture today means we can layer on exciting new features much faster in the future.
Below we’ve captured some of our work in progress. Nothing is final, but we wanted to share what we are cooking up so far. If you have feedback, keep reading on. At the bottom of the post we have  a link to a user research study where we want to hear from you and what you want to see from Thunderbird for iOS.
Hassle-free setup
Adding account user flow with options for email services like Google and Microsoft
We know people are really busy, often doing more than one thing at a time. We’re making login fast, secure, and fully automatic, so whether you’re signing in with a single click or setting up multiple accounts, you can get to your inbox quickly. 
Solid reliable connections
Thunderbird inbox
An email app is only as good as its connection. Behind the scenes, we’re building a background sync that maintains a steady connection with your provider that keeps your inbox up to date while respecting your battery life.
Core daily tools
Formatting toolbar (highlighted to show the details)
Your daily email routine should feel effortless. We’re polishing the essentials: a clutter-free, easy-to-read inbox layout paired with a clean, modern editor that lets you format messages smoothly without getting in your way.
Designed for growth
Thunderbird has always belonged to its community. We’re structuring the app with clean code and an experimental feature flag system so it’s easy for community developers to contribute. This means power users will be able to test out new experimental features early, and external contributors can easily help us extend what the app can do.
When can you try it?
Our goal is to have a first version ready for community testing in the next few months.
Building with our community, not just for people, is core to what we are trying to do. To help us decide what to build next after our first release, we’d love your input. If you had to pick the top three things that matter most to your daily email routine, what would they be?
➡️ Survey link
Update: the survey has now closed. Thanks to all that responded!
A note to the community 
Lastly, we know how long many of you have been asking for and waiting for Thunderbird on iOS. Whether you’ve dropped a comment on our forums, tagged us on social media, or simply kept an eye on our progress, thank you for your patience!
Bringing Thunderbird to iPhone and iPad isn’t just about building an app; it’s about doing it right so it serves you reliably for years to come. Today, we want to pop open the hood, share where we are, and work with everyone to design the best possible experience.

title: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
content:
The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
2 days ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Madison Chapman
Alexander Pomper
(Credit: Alexander Pomper)
Trevor Warmedahl has spent years documenting rare and traditional cheesemaking methods, and believes that "cheese is an edible manifestation of a place".
Trevor Warmedahl was working as a commercial cheesemaker in Seattle when he realised he was using milk that came from animals he never saw. So, he quit his job and set off on what has become a global odyssey to discover places that still make cheese the old-fashioned way. 
In 2019 he arrived in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and lived alone in a yurt with a dog as his companion. He soon discovered that dairy was sacred there: the women flicked milk into the air before cheesemaking, a gesture of respect called a milk libation. He visited homes where whey bubbled over central hearths and fresh, unripened byaslag cheese covered tables. After hiking to shrines, he noticed people offered dairy products as a symbol of purity.
As summer unfolded and city-dwellers migrated to the Mongolian steppe to farm, Warmedahl itched to join. He jumped on a Soviet-era coal-powered sleeper train for a rickety overnight ride across the Gobi Desert. On the journey back to Ulaanbaatar, he met a local who invited him to stay with her herder family on the Zavkhan grassland.
Trevor Warmedahl
Warmedahl spent time living in rural Mongolia and milking yaks (Credit: Trevor Warmedahl)
ADVERTISEMENT
Warmedahl spent that summer waking before dawn to milk yaks, chasing livestock up the valley on horses, listening to shepherds' folk songs at sunset and cooking milk into dehydrated, sweet-and-sour curds called aaruul. The experience inspired him to seek out other places preserving rare cheesemaking traditions before they disappeared.
During the past six years, Warmedahl has hitched, hiked and driven through more than 20 countries, documenting traditional cheesemaking and pastoral lifestyles, and offering workshops on natural dairy processing. After recently completing a 193km (120-mile) cheese trek across the Peaks of the Balkans Trail, he shared with the BBC what cheesemaking reveals about a place.
You've been to so many places – Bulgaria, Pakistan, Italy, Austria, Cambodia. Share a standout adventure. 
Ancestral cheeses in Georgia have no analogues – I call them "fossil cheeses" because they were almost lost but are making a comeback as part of a broader post-Soviet cultural revival. My pinnacle moment happened in Tusheti, a mountain region bordering Russia near the tourist village of Omalo.
The cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness
I showed up with vague directions to the shepherds' summer camp, which was deep in the valley. That's a theme: the cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness. It was drop-dead gorgeous, just me and my backpack. The valley ends on an abrupt cliff, with deteriorating medieval stone towers. Shepherds build their camps from the decay. I saw how these guys milked sheep by hand with wooden pails, rustic-style. It's a feta-like cheese called Tushuri guda, aged in inside-out sheepskins. At the end of the season, I walked about 130km (81 miles) back down the valley with them and 300 sheep. The herd has done this for generations – they know where to go. The shepherds just coordinated, and it created this crazy lawless feeling with dogs barking and me, chasing stray sheep down ravines.
Trevor Warmedahl
Warmedahl lived and worked in Tusheti, Georgia with shepherds (Credit: Trevor Warmedahl)
At night we'd build a campfire and drink, and even with the language barrier, we'd relate through food. Sometimes language isn't needed. In cheesemaking, if two hearts want to connect, they'll find a way.
How is cheese and cheesemaking a reflection of a community's history and culture? 
Cheese is a sensory experience and embodies larger ideas about how we live. It represents how meaningful human cultures can be. At its best, cheese reflects this complex relationship between humans, landscapes, microbial life and livestock at a time [when] we've become so separate from how food is made. And the cultural element holds the constellation together. 
Don't try something once, try it 10 times
The cheeses I highlight represent an older mentality, with a sense of stewardship over the places we live and farm. So, a little bit more of the wildness of nature slips into the product. [Cheese is] an edible manifestation of place, of cultural history transformed into delicious food. 
Why is cheesemaking especially important today? 
The diversity and range of cheese is infinite. When animals eat, they transform grass and entire landscapes into milk that becomes cheese, and animals can graze [almost] anywhere. So, it's a lifestyle that can move in response to climate uncertainty and desertification – real challenges today.
The cheeses I focus on – natural farmstead cheeses [made exclusively with milk from a farmer's own animals] – reflect deep, ethical relationships between people and livestock and highlight the incredible diversity of heritage livestock. With industrialisation, that diversity is vanishing at an alarming rate. So pastoral cheesemaking strikes me as profoundly sustainable.
Trevor Warmedahl
"Don't try something once, try it 10 times" (Credit: Trevor Warmedahl)
What can so-called "exotic cheeses" that challenge us reveal about a place? 
There's this greyish-brown cheese from Norway, gammelost, [covered in] moulds like fruit rot. It tastes like a musty cellar with bold, mouth-numbing spiciness. It wasn't for me. But deliciousness is cultural. It's taught. So, I always say: don't try something once, try it 10 times. Uncomfortable foods open doors. But be sure to eat them because you're interested in the culture, not because they're freaky to you.
One of the easiest ways to express interest in a culture is to say: feed me what you eat. When people realise you're genuine, the relationship deepens and you begin to understand their history through food. Funky cheeses become cultural emblems because of how obscure and special they are.
You set out on your global cheese journey without a real plan. What did this approach add to your experience?
Back then [in 2019], I was hopping on a whim from one volunteer gig to the next, drawn to remote places where people worked to protect and revitalise traditional cheeses. Workaway on farms, or staying for a while at guesthouses where cheese is made, are still amazing ways to go beyond tourism to see how people really live.
Cheese gives you access to a global community, like at [the Slow Food Cheese Festival in] Bra, Italy. But anything you can do to find that deeper experience – food, handicrafts – is worth it, even if you can't always plan in advance. If your heart is in the right place and you jump fully into adventure when it calls, the details will almost always work themselves out.  
Trevor Warmedahl
Warmedahl encourages responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism (Credit: Trevor Warmedahl)
What advice would you give fellow travellers about how to best experience unique cheeses abroad?
Find the cheese shop or cheesemonger that has the most local tilt and ask them which cheesemakers you can and should visit. Organising it yourself is cheaper. But there are also paid tours where you can experience a range of cheeses in a short period and really get to know a place. Just make sure that the cost actually supports local producers – that's what I call responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism.
How can other travellers seek out responsible agrotourism experiences?
Look for local cheesemakers and guides. It's also important to not expect farmers to sanitise things. It's normal to go to a farm and see broken-down equipment and mud. When we romanticise tradition, it encourages locals to put themselves in a museum. But tools [and] tradition have always evolved.
More like this:
• The elusive cheese with no recipe
• Is cheese the new reason to travel?
• The woman saving Georgia's lost cheeses
We need to be open to the fact that it's not all grandmas spinning wool on wheels outside stone cottages. Then it becomes kind of a show, and we're pushing farmers to become something they're not for tourists. 
What places have exciting, overlooked, or under-the-radar cheeses? Where are you keen to travel next?
Hands down, Turkey. It's a universe of cheese that doesn't get enough attention. Tulum peyniri is emblematic of pastoral lifestyles and the extreme sacrifice at the root of dairying and – I'd argue – life. That's because it's aged mainly in furry goatskins, so it looks insane because it can take on animal shapes. Somehow, I didn't think it would be delicious. How good can goatskin-aged cheese be, right? It was phenomenal. I was blown away by deep flavours and textures I'd never seen in cheese before.
Alamy
Tulum peyniri is a Turkish cheese that's aged in furry goatskins (Credit: Alamy)
Turkish cheese needs to be talked about alongside Western Europe. More remote places have just as many fascinating cheeses to preserve and celebrate.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
--

[BUG] bionic: wcscspn()/wcspbrk() treat every wchar_t >= 0x100 as a match (Android 17, CP3A.260905.009)
 #2260
New issue
Open
Description
francisdb
opened 2d agoon Oct 12, 2026
Last edited by francisdb
Description
On Android 17 builds from September 2026, wcscspn() and wcspbrk() stop at the first character of the string that is >= U+0100 whenever the reject set has two or more characters that are all < U+0100. The character is reported as a match even though it is not in the set. wcsspn(), wcschr(), wcsrchr(), wmemchr() and wcsstr() are correct.
Any code that scans wide strings for ASCII delimiters, for example newline or wildcard characters, breaks as soon as the text contains an emoji, CJK, Cyrillic, Greek or Latin Extended character.
Affected / unaffected
Device Build Result
Pixel 7 google/panther/panther:17/CP3A.260905.009/16091614:user/release-keys broken
Pixel 8a google/akita/akita:17/CP3A.260905.009/16091614:user/release-keys (patch 2026-09-05) broken
Nothing Phone 2 Nothing/PongEEA/Pong:16/BQ2A.250721.001-BP2A.250605.031.A3 (patch 2026-08-01) ok
The public android17-release sources (android-17.0.0_r1, June 2026) build wcscspn/wcspbrk from external/llvm-libc, which is a plain nested loop over wchar_t and is correct. The code on the September builds is different (see "Mechanism"), so the regression was introduced between the June and September releases.
Reproducer
Build with the NDK (aarch64-linux-android30-clang), push to /data/local/tmp, run with adb shell:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <wchar.h>

int main(void)
{
    wchar_t s[] = {'a', 0x1F680, 0x100, 'b', 'x', '\n', 0};
    printf("wcscspn(s, L\"x\\n\") = %zu (expected 4)\n", wcscspn(s, L"x\n"));
    printf("wcspbrk(s, L\"x\\n\") = index %ld (expected 4)\n", (long)(wcspbrk(s, L"x\n") - s));
    printf("wcsspn(s, L\"a\\U0001F680\") = %zu (expected 2)\n", wcsspn(s, L"a\U0001F680"));
    return 0;
}
Output on CP3A.260905.009:
wcscspn(s, L"x\n") = 1 (expected 4)
wcspbrk(s, L"x\n") = index 1 (expected 4)
wcsspn(s, L"a\U0001F680") = 2 (expected 2)
A sweep of every code point from U+0001 to U+10FFFF (skipping surrogates and the two set members) with wcscspn(L"<cp>\n", L"x\n") returns 0 instead of 1 for 1,111,808 code points: every one from U+0100 to U+10FFFF. U+0001 to U+00FF are correct.
Which set shapes trigger it (all measured on the Pixel 8a):
Reject set Result
one character ok
two or more characters, all < U+0100 (e.g. L"x\n", L"\xe9\n") broken
two or more characters, at least one >= U+0100 ok
haystack limited to U+0080..U+00FF ok
Mechanism (from the shipped libc.so)
Disassembly of wcscspn in /apex/com.android.runtime/lib64/bionic/libc.so on CP3A.260905.009 shows three paths selected by the set:
One character: a plain compare loop. Correct.
Two or more characters: a 256-byte bool table on the stack is filled from the set while the set characters are in 1..0xFF. If a set character >= 0x100 is seen, the function falls back to calling wcschr() for each haystack character. Correct.
Otherwise the haystack is scanned against the table:
a2564:  ldrb  w8, [x9, x8]        ; table[c]
a2568:  tbnz  w8, #0, a2578       ; in set -> stop (correct)
a256c:  ldr   w8, [x22, #0x4]!    ; next character
a2570:  cmp   w8, #0x100
a2574:  b.lo  a2564               ; c < 0x100 -> keep scanning
a2578:  ...                       ; c >= 0x100 -> STOP, reported as a match
A character >= 0x100 cannot be in a set whose members are all < 0x100, so for wcscspn the scan must continue past it. The code stops instead. wcsspn has the same structure, and there stopping is the correct answer (the character is not in the keep set), which is why only the complement functions are wrong. wcspbrk is implemented on top of this scan and inherits the bug.
The existing bionic test TEST(wchar, wcspbrk) in tests/wchar_test.cpp only uses ASCII input, so it does not catch this. A test such as EXPECT_EQ(3u, wcscspn(L"aĀb\n", L"x\n")) would.
Real-world impact
Visual Pinball on Android (libwinevbs, a Unix build of Wine's vbscript engine) stopped loading any table whose VBScript source contains a comment with an emoji after the September update: the lexer uses wcspbrk(ptr, L"\n\r") to skip comments, got the position of the first emoji instead of the line end, and reported "Invalid character". FileSystem.MoveFolder likewise treated every path containing a character >= U+0100 as a wildcard pattern via wcspbrk(src, L"*?><").
Worked around downstream by replacing the calls with plain loops: vpinball/libwinevbs#41 (shipped in vpinball/vpinball@e7837322f4).
Full disassembly of the affected functions and the probe sources are available on request.
I am using a supported NDK
I have checked and the NDK I'm using is currently supported
Affected versions

title: Sound – Bartosz Ciechanowski
content:
October 18, 2022
Sound
Invisible and relentless, sound is seemingly just there, traveling through our surroundings to carry beautiful music or annoying noises. In this article I’ll explain what sound is, how it’s created and propagated.
Throughout this presentation you will be hearing different sounds, which you will often play yourself on little keyboards like the one below. You can either click its keys with your mouse or use WER keys on your computer keyboard, but before you do so make sure your system volume is at a reasonable level:
W
220 Hz
E
330 Hz
R
440 Hz
We’ll eventually understand how these sounds are created and how they get to your ears, but we have to start by talking about the medium that is most commonly associated with sound – air.
Air
You’re probably aware that at microscopic level air consists of individual, tiny particles. Let’s look at the behavior of those molecules up close. In the demonstration below, I parceled out a tiny cube of air – notice how the molecules freely enter and leave this space. You can drag the cube around to change the viewing angle and you can also control the speed of the flow of time with the slider:
I need to note that this visualization simplifies things a little. The air consists primarily of nitrogen and oxygen – their particles contain two atoms bound together, but for simplicity I’m drawing all molecules as simple spheres.
Each particle of air travels through space with some velocity in a more or less random direction. While some molecules are faster, and some are slower, at room temperature the average velocity of a particle is a staggering 1510 ft/s so to make the particles visible I’m showing their motion significantly slowed down. As a side note, I’m using imperial units here, but you can switch to the metric system if you prefer.
With all the commotion in the previous simulation it may have been hard to see that the air particles collide with each other. In the demonstration below, I’m flashing the particles red and making them a little bigger right after they collide. To make these events easier to see you can control the speed of time with the slider:
Naturally, those particles can also collide with other things in the environment. In the simulation below I put up walls around that parcel of air. While at this scale we could also see the individual atoms constituting the walls of the box, I’m not showing them here to make things clearer. The particles of air are bouncing off these sides and every time that happens I’m drawing a little blue glow on the wall:
When an air particle bounces off, it imparts a small force on the wall. Although a single collision doesn’t do that much, with enough particles present the walls experience a constant barrage of collisions which exert expanding pressure on the container. The magnitude of that pressure is the sum of all these forces of impacts divided by the area of the box. Intuitively, for a box of a fixed size, the more particles there are, the heavier they are, and the faster they move, the higher the pressure.
Let’s see what happens if we resize this box a little while keeping the number of particles constant. In the demonstration below, you can drag the slider to change the length of the box, the plot in the bottom tracks the number of collisions per area of the box in a unit of time:
The number of collisions per area, and thus the pressure, increases as we squeeze particles closer together, and it decreases as we let them loose. Remember that we’re observing a significantly slowed down simulation. Because of the speeds involved here, I’m only letting you resize the box at a limited pace. That limitation prevents the walls from moving at enormous speeds, which would create some truly extreme pressure conditions.
It may not be immediately clear, but the experience of pressure is not limited to the walls of the box we built. Molecules in any open region of gas also experience compressing forces exerted by collisions with molecules from the neighboring regions. Those collisions aren’t as neatly aligned in space, but in aggregate it makes no difference if particles are bouncing off a wall or off particles from the neighboring area – the pressure is still there.
All the collisions between particles also have other consequences, but to look at them I need to adjust the scale at which we’ll be looking at – you can do this with a slider below:
The small cube of air from the previous demonstration is now just part of a larger volume. While this large cube is 20 times larger in each dimension, its sides measure only 1 micrometer – a few times smaller than a width of spider silk. Unfortunately, it would be both chaotic to display and taxing to correctly simulate the over 26 million air particles that one could find in this area. Instead, I’ll just visualize the motion of a single molecule as it travels through this space. In the demonstration below, I enlarged that particle to make it visible, you can also control the flow of time with the slider:
Due to collisions with other molecules, it may take a while for this particle to travel a significant distance and get out of this larger volume. You probably experienced this yourself – when someone sprays perfume in a distant part of a room the scent doesn’t instantly get to you. It’s only after some lucky aromatic particles manage to bounce into the vicinity of your nose that you get to experience the smell. If it wasn’t for the collisions with other molecules, those fragrant particles could travel the distance to your nose in a fraction of a second.
The important point is that, while the air particles move very fast, the collisions with other particles keep them mostly contained inside their local area. Over a longer period of time they will eventually all mix up, but at the short timeframes we’ll be interested in here, each reasonably sized parcel of air contains mostly the same particles.
All the microscopic behavior of individual particles we’ve observed ends up contributing to properties of air at larger scales. From this point on, we’ll move past looking at individual molecules and instead we’ll focus on regions of air that more closely match the sizes we’re used to. Those particles are still there, and they’re what actually end up distributing changes in gases, but we need to aggregate a huge collection of the molecules to end up with more discernible motions.
Let’s witness some of this large scale behavior when a section of air in a tube gets pushed on by a moving plate. In the demonstration below, I divided the air next to that circular plate into individual slices, which I’m drawing with thin lines. Although these boundaries are imaginary, they let us see what happens to different sections of air as you move the plate around with the slider:
Notice that the individual parcels of air move only a little from their initial position, but the disturbance caused by the motion of the plate seems to propagate through them with some speed. Moreover, that disturbance moves away from the plate regardless of the direction of the plate’s motion.
If you recall our experiment with a resized cube of air having more or less available space, you’ll notice that a very similar situation happens here inside each slice – this tells us that we’re witnessing some changes in pressure.
Let’s look at this situation from the side, which will make it easier to see how these pressure changes propagate. In the following demonstration I’m coloring each slice of air red when it’s compressed and the pressure increases, and I’m coloring it blue when it’s expanded and the pressure decreases:
When the plate moves to the right, it compresses the air particles in its vicinity, which increases the pressure in this region. Those particles then push and expand into particles in the neighboring slice of air, which then push onto the next slice and so on. All of this results in an area of higher pressure propagating away from the plate.
On the flip side, when the plate moves to the left, it creates an area of depletion, or rarefaction, which the neighboring slice of air rushes to fill in. This then reduces the pressure in the vicinity of the next slice and so on. While the slices move towards the receding plate, the pressure disturbance still moves away from the plate.
What we’ve just seen more clearly were pressure waves propagating through the air. When those pressure waves reach our ears we perceive them as sound. By moving the plate we’ve effectively created a very crude speaker that emits sounds as its moving element changes position.
While this simple demonstration helps to build an intuitive understanding of the propagation of pressure waves, the relation between the vibration of the object and the pressure disturbances it generates is much more complicated. We’ll soon explore some of those details, but for now we’ll focus on the relation between the movement of that vibrating element and the sound it produces.
Making Sounds
Let’s begin by introducing a simple musical instrument. By pressing a key down, you can request the plate to rapidly change its position. When you let that key go, the plate will move back by the same amount. Notice that each of the three keys moves the plate by a different amount, with red marker showing the total offset:
W
E
R
Despite its simplicity, this device lets us observe a few things. Firstly, a sudden jump of a plate creates a popping sound. It also doesn’t matter if the object has jumped forwards or backwards – the effect sounds the same.
Secondly, the loudness of that pop depends on the magnitude of the jump – the larger the jump the louder the pop.
Finally, this plate can jump forwards or backwards from any position – you can verify this by holding one of the keys and then pressing some other key. That pop sounds exactly the same as the sound created by a standalone key press.
Three pops of different loudness is not much to create music with as this only lets us play some simple beats. You may have tried pressing the buttons as fast as possible to create more upbeat tunes, but there are limits to how fast human fingers can press buttons.
Thankfully, we can ask the device you’re using to repeat the pops at a certain rate. In the demonstration below, you can drag the first slider to change how many times per second the plate should jump forwards and backwards. You can also control how far the plate moves with each jump using the second slider:
To describe the frequency of vibration, I’m using the unit of hertz, often abbreviated as Hz – it describes how many full cycles of motion happen within a single second. For example, a frequency of 2 Hz means that two full cycles happened in a second which means that the plate moved back and forth and back and forth again.
While at lower frequencies these patterns sound like a rapid series of pops, at higher frequencies these sounds blend together into a discernible note. The most important observation we can make here is that the higher the frequency with which the plate vibrates, the higher the perceived pitch of the resulting sound is.
You’ve probably observed that at lower rates you could follow the motion of the vibrating plate, but as the frequency increases, it becomes impossible to reliably track its movement. Unfortunately, we’re hitting the limits of frequencies we can easily display on a screen and perceive with our eyes, so from this point on I’ll significantly slow down the motion of the plate. The patterns of motion will still be correct, they’ll just happen at a much slower pace so that we can actually see what’s going on.
With that in mind, let’s make our music synthesizer create those very frequent jumps of the plate. We’ll assign a different frequency to each key – you can see them displayed above the keys. I’m also drawing three plots corresponding to each key, and an additional plot showing the cumulative effect of the individual motions.
These plots, or waveforms, represent the motion of the plate as requested by the keys. As the plots pass through the center line they reflect the current position of the plate, but remember that the motions we see here are a few hundred times slower than the actual ones:
W
E
R
Notice that when you press two keys at the same time you can still hear both sounds playing through – we’ve already seen that the final plate movement is just the sum of individual motions that each key requests.
You may also have realized that I’ve shifted the center line of the plate. What we consider a base position of that object is ultimately arbitrary. The keys simply request the plate to move forward or backward and they don’t care from where it’s starting, but having the object oscillate around a well defined origin will be more convenient.
If you look closely at the plots when two keys are pressed, you may have also noticed that there are some areas where one of the keys wants the plate to move forward, while the other wants it to move back. As a result, the plate stays at the same position.
What may be a little surprising is that there is nothing magical about the sound emitted by the plate when two keys are pressed – the emitted sound depends purely on the final movement of the plate. In the demonstration below, I made the third key emit the same pattern of motion as the combination of the first two:
W
E
R
The sound emitted when the third key is pressed is exactly the same as the sound emitted when the first two keys are pressed together. This is a very important observation, as it lets us explore some other patterns of motion that the keys could induce.
We’ll expand on this idea by changing the way in which the plate vibrates. Instead of having it rapidly jump back and forth, we can request the plate to move with constant velocity, following a triangular pattern. Let’s look at that pattern up close. Like other periodic shapes, a triangular waveform can be characterized by its amplitude, frequency, and phase:
In these visual examples the amplitude controls the height of the waveform. The frequency controls the width of the repeating pattern, which affects how many repetitions of the up-and-down triangles can fit inside a single second. The phase just shifts the shape around to change what we consider the beginning of that pattern.
We’ve already seen how the amplitude of the plate’s motion affects the perceived loudness, and this triangular motion is no different. In the demonstration below, all three keys move the plate in the same pattern, only their amplitude is different:
W
E
R
Similarly to the original rectangular pattern, we perceive different frequencies of this triangular motion as different pitches. In the following demonstration, each key has a different frequency as marked by the display in the upper part of the keyboard. The higher the frequency the higher the perceived pitch:
W
E
R

title: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts
content:
Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts
By Bill Toulas
October 12, 2026 12:27 PM 1
Ledger has confirmed that some of its devices distributed through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with a hardware implant that drained users' cryptocurrency wallets.
The company has been investigating reports of users losing funds from wallets purchased through CryptoBilis, a major Malaysia-based hardware wallet retailer operating across Southeast Asia.
Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware.
Ledger wallets are physical devices designed to securely store the private keys that control cryptocurrency assets and authorize transactions.
On October 9, Ledger said it had launched an investigation into user reports of cryptocurrency losses and asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices.
The next day, the company confirmed hardware tampering on at least one device, though it’s still unclear exactly how or when the devices were tampered with.
"Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger is reaching out to impacted users as part of the ongoing investigation," Ledger said.
The crypto wallet maker also noted that it was working with authorities to identify the perpetrator and bring them to justice.
“[...]Ledger recommends users who purchased a Ledger device from this reseller to not initiate set up if they have not yet done so. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with a new seed),” warned Ledger.
Yesterday, Ledger provided another update, confirming that all user reports of unexpected fund drains were linked to devices sold through CryptoBilis and describing the affected volume as “limited.”
While the company did not disclose the type of devices compromised in this supply-chain attack, reports online talk about a spy implant in Ledger X devices that blends with the legitimate hardware.
Mark Karpelès, currently leading Karpeles Lab Inc. and CTO at Shells.com, showed a picture of the new implant in Ledger X, saying that it was "quite an evolution" from previous versions featuring manually soldered wires.
Hardware implant inside Ledger X device
source: Mark Karpelès
The former CEO of Mt. Gox said the implant was concealed behind the screen, but its antenna cable would have indicated that something was wrong.
According to Karpelès, the malicious hardware captured the device's display output and button presses to identify the seed phrase, then transmitted it to the attacker over an LTE connection using an eSIM.
"Ledger Nano X are used to store crypto. The spy implants are used to steal whatever crypto you store in those Ledger Nano X," Karpelès explained.
Although the CEO did not name CryptoBilis as the vendor of the compromised LedgerX, he said the device was not purchased via Ledger's recommended channels but from "a well known platform via a Chinese seller (product shipped from Malaysia)."
Tibane Labs, a cryptocurrency research and development studio, confirmed Karpelès' finding, adding that there were two implant versions for Ledger X.
The researchers obtained two variants, one in a Ledger device bought on Amazon Japan from " China-based seller · shipped from Malaysia," the other purchased on Yahoo! Auctions, Japan.
In a report over the weekend, Tibane Labs notes that the threat actor made room for the malicious circuitry by replacing the original battery with a smaller one, which powers both the implant and the Ledger X.
"Under the battery and antenna sits an ST STM32G431KBU6 (Arm Cortex‑M4, 128 KB flash, UFQFPN‑32)," the researchers found inside one of the devices.
For connectivity, the actor used "a tiny eSIM, an 8‑pad package just 2×2 mm, next to the MCU, and a shielded LTE module that sends the words out."
In the second hardware wallet analyzed, Tibane researchers found that markings on both the MCU (Microcontroller Unit) and the eSIM had been scraped off to hide the part numbers.
The second variant, which appears to be the same one that Karpelès described, is more advanced. It ran on the original battery and fit into the space normally occupied by the foam padding under the OLED display.
In both cases, the tell tale was the antenna wire, which ran along the top edge in the case of the second implant. In the first implant, the antenna is taped across the top of the battery and the shielded LTE module.
Hardware implant inside Ledger X
source: Tibane Labs
The researchers warned that the specimen above used "a designed, panelised flex PCB, the kind ordered from a board house, not a hand-built one-off."
Ledger is advising users to avoid purchasing from unauthorized resellers as they run an increased risk of getting counterfeit or modified devices.
The company is also reminding its authorized resellers and distributors to get the products only through authorized channels and to avoid restocking returned products.
Ledger provides a ‘Genuine Check’ mechanism to determine the authenticity of the device; however, it explicitly warns that it cannot detect added implants when the device’s original Secure Element remains intact.
At this time, there’s no indication that any other Ledger resellers are shipping compromised wallets; however, the community’s trust in the resellers’ network has been compromised, with many now calling for its dismantling.

title: Press-Release
content:
Press Release
An Important Update About Grace Hopper Celebration
It is with deep regret that we are announcing the cancellation of this year’s Grace Hopper Celebration in Anaheim, CA.
This is not a decision we made lightly; we understand it leaves many of our community disappointed. It is a function of not having the funds required to move forward with the Celebration, unlike in years past. Unlike past events, this year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below our expectations and, ultimately, below the level needed to cover critical operating expenses.
We know this decision affects far more than an event. Many of you have made travel arrangements, booked hotels, received visas, secured time away from work, organized teams, and planned important moments around being together. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this creates.
If you have plans to attend GHC, please take the following steps now:
Cancel or modify your airline, train, or other travel reservations directly with your travel provider.
Cancel hotel reservations made independently directly with the hotel or booking provider, and any other reservations or commitments connected to your trip.
Information regarding GHC registration, sponsorships, exhibitor commitments, and other financial matters will be communicated directly to the individuals and organizations affected. AnitaB.org will contact registrants about registration fees by October 26. We recognize that each person’s circumstances may be different.
For questions or assistance specifically related to the cancellation, please contact [GHC@AnitaB.org]. We ask that you use this address so we can centralize inquiries and respond as effectively as possible.
To our attendees, sponsors, speakers, volunteers, partners, and everyone who has invested in making Grace Hopper Celebration possible: we are profoundly grateful, and profoundly sorry.
GHC has always been about more than a place or a moment on the calendar. It is about a community that has spent decades opening doors, expanding opportunity, and making sure women technologists have a voice in shaping the future of technology.
GHC has been central to our mission, and the circumstances leading to its cancellation have adversely affected our finances. We are evaluating strategic alternatives and the type of programming we can offer in the future. I anticipate further announcements will be made in the coming weeks as we gain greater clarity on key variables.
Brenda Darden Wilkerson
President & CEO
AnitaB.org
Frequently Asked Questions
